IN THE CHAIR: ESTEBAN GONZÁLEZ PONS

Vice-President

2-0218-0000.sourceText:
Señor presidente, no hay debate únicamente sobre un acuerdo comercial.

Hoy decidimos qué lugar quiere ocupar Europa en un mundo cada vez más dominado por la confrontación, el proteccionismo y las políticas de poder. Tras más de una década de negociaciones, la Unión Europea y México culminan una decisión geopolítica de primer orden: modernizar nuestro Acuerdo Global.

Este Acuerdo es mucho más que la eliminación de aranceles o la apertura de mercados. Es una respuesta política a quienes creen que el siglo XXI debe organizarse mediante amenazas, guerras comerciales, coerción económica o zonas de influencia.

Nosotros defendemos otra lógica con este Acuerdo Global: defendemos reglas frente a fuerza, cooperación frente a la confrontación, y Derecho internacional frente al unilateralismo. En un momento en el que algunos levantan muros, utilizan aranceles como armas y cuestionan décadas de construcción multilateral, Europa y México envían un mensaje distinto al mundo: más cooperación, más instituciones, más Derecho internacional y más comercio predecible con altos estándares medioambientales, sociales y laborales.

La alternativa al multilateralismo no es más soberanía, es la ley de la selva. En este contexto, Europa necesita socios fiables, socios democráticos, socios capaces de aportar estabilidad institucional, capacidad industrial, seguridad jurídica y compromiso con un orden internacional basado en normas.

Hay pocos en el mundo que combinan todos estos elementos como lo hace México. México es una potencia económica, industrial, tecnológica y diplomática de primerísimo orden. Es un miembro del G20 y uno de los socios estratégicos más importantes de la Unión Europea. Pero no solo eso: es una sociedad con una fuerte identidad propia, profunda y milenaria; una nación heredera de hondas raíces culturales ricas, diversas y vibrantes.

México es un país que ha sabido convertir su diversidad, mestizaje y pluralidad en una fuente de fortaleza nacional. Europa no mira a México únicamente como un mercado. Europa mira a México con respeto, nunca desde el reduccionismo, el paternalismo o la ignorancia, porque compartimos principios esenciales: la defensa de la Carta de las Naciones Unidas o el compromiso con la soberanía de los Estados. Compartimos la convicción de que ninguna potencia tiene derecho a imponer su voluntad sobre otros mediante la coerción económica o la fuerza. Compartimos la certeza de que los grandes desafíos a los que nos enfrentamos —la lucha contra las desigualdades, el cambio climático o la transición energética o digital— deben hacerse mediante cooperación, no haciendo de menos o mediante la confrontación.

Quiero destacar hoy aquí que la determinación de la presidenta Von der Leyen y del presidente Costa nos ha permitido llegar hasta aquí. También nos lo ha permitido la decisión estratégica de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, por su liderazgo sereno, tranquilo y firme en la escena internacional.

Abrimos una nueva etapa de oportunidades compartidas para una prosperidad compartida.

Hoy que hablamos de las relaciones entre la Unión Europea y México, quiero recalcar que cuando Europa atravesó momentos oscuros durante el siglo XX, México abrió sus puertas a quienes huían de la guerra y de la persecución política; ofreció refugio, dignidad y esperanza. Y algunos —especialmente en España, por la acogida del exilio republicano español— tenemos un sentimiento de deber y gratitud con México que permanece.

Por eso, hoy hacemos algo más que aprobar un Acuerdo. Defendemos una idea del mundo. La idea de que la cooperación es más poderosa que el conflicto, de que las reglas son preferibles a la arbitrariedad, de que la apertura es más inteligente que el repliegue, y de que frente al nacionalismo económico, el proteccionismo y la política del poder, Europa debe responder construyendo alianzas con quienes creen en la democracia, el Derecho internacional y el multilateralismo.

Con este Acuerdo se trata de defender una idea del orden internacional, un orden basado en normas y no en amenazas, en cooperación y no en coerción, en relaciones entre socios y no vasallos. Ese es el verdadero significado de este Acuerdo. Y por eso hay que respaldarlo con convicción.
2-0218-0000.englishText:
Mr President, the debate is not solely about a trade agreement.

Today we decide what place Europe wants to occupy in a world increasingly dominated by confrontation, protectionism and power politics. After more than a decade of negotiations, the European Union and Mexico are culminating a first-order geopolitical decision: modernizing our Global Agreement.

This Agreement is much more than the elimination of tariffs or the opening of markets. It is a political response to those who believe that the 21st century should be organized through threats, trade wars, economic coercion or spheres of influence.

We defend a different logic with this Global Agreement: we defend rules over force, cooperation over confrontation, and international law over unilateralism. At a time when some are building walls, using tariffs as weapons and questioning decades of multilateral construction, Europe and Mexico are sending a different message to the world: more cooperation, more institutions, more international law and more predictable trade with high environmental, social and labor standards.

 The alternative to multilateralism is not more sovereignty, it is the law of the jungle. In this context, Europe needs reliable partners, democratic partners, partners capable of providing institutional stability, industrial capacity, legal certainty and a commitment to a rules-based international order.

There are few in the world that combine all these elements the way Mexico does. Mexico is an economic, industrial, technological and diplomatic power of the very first order. It is a G20 member and one of the European Union's most important strategic partners. But not only that: it is a society with a strong, deep and millenary identity of its own; a nation heir to deep cultural roots that are rich, diverse and vibrant.

Mexico is a country that has known how to turn its diversity, mestizaje and plurality into a source of national strength. Europe does not look at Mexico solely as a market. Europe looks at Mexico with respect, never from reductionism, paternalism or ignorance, because we share essential principles: the defense of the United Nations Charter or the commitment to the sovereignty of States. We share the conviction that no power has the right to impose its will on others through economic coercion or force. We share the certainty that the great challenges we face—the fight against inequalities, climate change, or the energy or digital transition—must be done through cooperation, not by belittling or through confrontation.

I want to highlight here today that the determination of President Von der Leyen and President Costa has allowed us to get here. It has also been allowed by the strategic decision of President Claudia Sheinbaum, for her serene, calm and firm leadership on the international scene.

We are opening a new stage of shared opportunities for shared prosperity.

Today as we speak about relations between the European Union and Mexico, I want to emphasize that when Europe went through dark moments during the 20th century, Mexico opened its doors to those fleeing war and political persecution; it offered refuge, dignity and hope. And some of us—especially in Spain, due to the reception of the Spanish republican exile—have a feeling of duty and gratitude toward Mexico that remains.

Therefore, today we are doing more than approving an Agreement. We are defending an idea of the world. The idea that cooperation is more powerful than conflict, that rules are preferable to arbitrariness, that openness is smarter than retreat, and that in the face of economic nationalism, protectionism and power politics, Europe must respond by building alliances with those who believe in democracy, international law and multilateralism.

With this Agreement it is about defending an idea of the international order, an order based on rules and not threats, on cooperation and not coercion, on relations between partners and not vassals. That is the true meaning of this Agreement. And that is why it must be supported with conviction.

2-0219-0000.sourceText:
Señor presidente, el Acuerdo Global con México va a ser una realidad. Es un punto de inflexión en una realidad que comenzó hace 25 años. Desde entonces, el comercio ha crecido un 148 %. Hoy supera los 82 000 millones de euros. No es una cifra abstracta: es industria, es empresa, es inversión, es competitividad, pero el mundo cambia rápido. Estamos en un contexto de fragmentación global, con tensiones comerciales, con amenazas recurrentes de nuevos aranceles. Europa no se puede quedar atrás. Necesitamos diversificar, más socios, más autonomía estratégica. Cuanto más comercio, más libre es la Unión. 25 años después de la modernización de nuestras relaciones comerciales, esta es más necesaria que nunca.

Los beneficios económicos son claros. La Unión y México suman más de 580 millones de consumidores. Es un mercado enorme. Las exportaciones europeas pueden crecer hasta un 75 %. Más de 45 000 empresas europeas se beneficiarán —la mayoría de ellas pymes— y el PIB de la Unión Europea puede aumentar en 1 800 millones de euros solo por la firma del Acuerdo. También es una buena noticia para nuestro sector agroalimentario. No debemos tener miedo: sectores como el porcino o el queso ganan, se eliminan aranceles y se protegen 568 indicaciones geográficas.

Además, es el primer acuerdo que incorpora una cláusula anticorrupción. Esto es clave si queremos inversiones transparentes y seguridad jurídica. Es también fundamental la incorporación de un sistema de tribunales de inversión permanente.

México y la Unión Europea comparten mucho: siglos de historia. Una historia compleja, profunda, que ha dado lugar a vínculos humanos, tradiciones, cultura, lengua. Todo ello forma parte de nuestra identidad.

Hoy decidimos sellar un destino común; hoy damos un paso más en nuestra relación. Este Acuerdo se basa en la confianza —confianza mutua— entre dos pueblos amigos que se aprecian y se respetan. Una relación así exige honestidad, la misma que entre buenos amigos. Y esa honestidad exige sinceridad, que nos hablemos claro, de lo que nos gusta y lo que no nos gusta tanto. Y hay cuestiones que nos preocupan, de forma sincera. La reforma del sistema judicial: la elección popular de todos los jueces genera serias dudas, debilita la separación de poderes. Sin estabilidad institucional no hay confianza, sin confianza no hay crecimiento. Nos preocupa la seguridad: 90 homicidios al día, impunidad del 94 %, el país con más periodistas asesinados, un crimen organizado que sabemos que ha permeado la sociedad y la economía. No podemos mirar hacia otro lado, fundamentalmente porque es un enorme drama humano, pero también económico. Y lamentamos profundamente, desde una perspectiva comercial, que el capítulo energético haya quedado fuera del Acuerdo. Esto va a dar lugar a vacíos regulatorios y desincentiva la inversión. Confiamos en que esta cuestión se pueda resolver pronto.

Somos amigos, somos socios y este Acuerdo sienta las bases para reafirmar nuestra relación. Una relación comercial ambiciosa, una relación política profunda, pero también una relación basada en el Estado de Derecho, en la independencia judicial, en la seguridad jurídica y en el respeto de los valores democráticos. Porque el comercio prospera cuando existen instituciones fuertes. La inversión llega cuando hay confianza.

Señorías, digamos sí a un Acuerdo fundamental para Europa: reforcemos nuestra posición global, mejoremos la competitividad, ampliemos alianzas. Cuanto más comercio, más libre será la Unión.
2-0219-0000.englishText:
Mr President, the Global Agreement with Mexico is going to become a reality. It is a turning point in a reality that began 25 years ago. Since then, trade has grown by 148%. Today it exceeds 82 billion euros. This is not an abstract figure: it is industry, business, investment, competitiveness, but the world is changing fast. We are in a context of global fragmentation, with trade tensions, with recurring threats of new tariffs. Europe cannot afford to fall behind. We need to diversify, more partners, more strategic autonomy. The more trade, the freer the Union is. 25 years after the modernisation of our trade relations, this is more necessary than ever.

The economic benefits are clear. The Union and Mexico together account for more than 580 million consumers. It is a huge market. European exports can grow by up to 75%. More than 45,000 European companies will benefit — the majority of them SMEs — and the GDP of the European Union can increase by 1.8 billion euros simply through the signing of the Agreement. It is also good news for our agri-food sector. We must not be afraid: sectors such as pork or cheese win, tariffs are eliminated and 568 geographical indications are protected.

Furthermore, it is the first agreement to incorporate an anti-corruption clause. This is key if we want transparent investments and legal certainty. The incorporation of a permanent investment court system is also fundamental.

Mexico and the European Union share a great deal: centuries of history. A complex, deep history that has given rise to human ties, traditions, culture, language. All of this forms part of our identity.

Today we decide to seal a common destiny; today we take a further step in our relationship. This Agreement is based on trust — mutual trust — between two friendly peoples who appreciate and respect each other. Such a relationship demands honesty, the same as between good friends. And that honesty demands sincerity, that we speak plainly to one another, about what we like and what we do not like quite as much. And there are issues that concern us, sincerely. The reform of the judicial system: the popular election of all judges raises serious doubts, it weakens the separation of powers. Without institutional stability there is no trust, without trust there is no growth. We are concerned about security: 90 homicides a day, 94% impunity, the country with the most murdered journalists, an organised crime that we know has permeated society and the economy. We cannot look the other way, fundamentally because it is an enormous human drama, but also an economic one. And we deeply regret, from a commercial perspective, that the energy chapter has been left out of the Agreement. This will give rise to regulatory gaps and disincentivises investment. We trust that this issue can be resolved soon.

We are friends, we are partners and this Agreement lays the foundations to reaffirm our relationship. An ambitious trade relationship, a deep political relationship, but also a relationship based on the Rule of Law, judicial independence, legal certainty and respect for democratic values. Because trade prospers when strong institutions exist. Investment arrives when there is trust.

Ladies and gentlemen, let us say yes to a fundamental Agreement for Europe: let us reinforce our global position, improve competitiveness, expand alliances. The more trade, the freer the Union will be.

2-0220-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, honourable Members, dear rapporteurs, trade is fundamental to the European Union economy, and we just heard an eloquent statement in this regard by the Taoiseach, who is heading the Irish Presidency, in the earlier debate. Why? Because more than 700 000 EU companies export beyond our borders and they support more than 30 million jobs across the Union, contributing in one way or another to almost half of our European GDP, not least thanks to our 45 free trade agreements with 81 countries covering more than half of our trade.

Yet the context for the EU trade policy has become increasingly unpredictable and volatile. We are witnessing deliberate disruptions of global trade and the weaponisation of dependencies. In such turbulent times, we need to work even more closely with our partners in key markets open, as well as new markets, for our exports, and diversify sources of imports for the European Union producers.

During this Commission's mandate, we have struck landmark deals with Mexico, Mercosur, Indonesia, India, Australia and Eastern and Southern African – so-called ESA – countries. We are also continuing to negotiate with the Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia and the United Arab Emirates. Against this background, let me turn now to the subject of today's debate: EU-Mexico trade relations.

The commercial ties between the EU and Mexico are already strong. We have been trading on preferential terms since the year 2000, when the trade pillar of the EU-Mexico Global Agreement entered into force. That has seen the bilateral trade in goods increase by 330 % in the last 25 years, while the trade in services has also expanded significantly, and the EU has become the second most important investor in Mexico.

But in the past two decades, the world has changed, which is why we needed a modernised agreement that takes EU-Mexico relations to a new level, establishing a modern and ambitious framework for bilateral trade and investment. It will make almost all EU-Mexico trade in goods tariff free. And this is especially important for the EU agri-food exporters as duties will be removed on nearly all key products.

While Europe's flagship food and drink products are protected under 569 geographical indications, the agreement will also support growth in EU services exports in sectors such as financial services, transport and e-commerce. It will reduce non-tariff barriers and help ensure a level playing field, including through stronger provisions on intellectual property rights.

It will strengthen cooperation on critical raw materials and support the competitiveness of the European industry. It will promote the digital transition on both sides through the dedicated chapter on digital trade, and it will make it easier for small and medium-sized enterprises to trade and invest. It will expand opportunities for EU firms in Mexico's public procurement market and it will help address practical difficulties faced by our investors in Mexico.

As you have underlined in the interim report accompanying this debate, the EU and Mexico are like-minded, long-standing partners. This agreement will deepen that partnership and strengthen our ability to work together on global challenges.

It also underlines our commitment to fair trade, shared prosperity, sustainability and rules-based cooperation, and it promotes sustainable development through legally binding commitments on labour rights, environmental protection, climate change and responsible business conduct in the TSD chapter, as well as on trade and gender equality and women's economic empowerment.

With the modernised agreement, we are better equipped to seize new opportunities and address common challenges, both bilaterally and at the multilateral level. So, honourable Members, this debate is an opportunity to send a clear message to Europeans and to our partners that Europe believes in fair trade, strong alliances and strategic openness, and that, when it comes to Mexico, we choose partnership and mutual benefit.

So I would kindly ask for your support to back this agreement, and I would conclude by thanking all of you for attending this debate and our two rapporteurs for great cooperation.

2-0221-0000.englishText:
Mr President, the European Union-Mexico Agreement is much more than a trade agreement. It is a strategic choice.

Mexico is the European Union's second largest trading partner in Latin America. More than 45,000 European companies export to Mexico, many of them small and medium-sized enterprises that will benefit from clearer rules, greater predictability and new investment opportunities.

These challenges are not external to the agreement; they are part of the conditions that determine whether the agreement will be credible, effective and sustainable.

There is no true economic predictability and trust for businesses without solid institutions. This Parliament recognizes and supports the agreement, but demands clear and verifiable commitments regarding the rule of law.

2-0222-0000.sourceText:
Señor presidente, señor comisario, este Parlamento está a punto de dar su consentimiento a un Acuerdo que ha tardado casi diez años en negociarse. Un Acuerdo que llega en un momento en el que el comercio global ya no puede entenderse únicamente en términos económicos.

Hoy, la Unión Europea es más consciente que nunca de que la política comercial es un pilar fundamental para nuestra seguridad económica y nuestra autonomía estratégica. Somos conscientes de la necesidad de diversificar nuestras relaciones comerciales y fortalecer alianzas con socios que comparten nuestro compromiso con el multilateralismo y con un comercio global basado en normas.

México es, sin duda, uno de los mejores ejemplos de esa clase de aliados estratégicos. Por eso, la firma del Acuerdo Global Modernizado entre la Unión Europea y México es una grandísima noticia que este Parlamento tiene que acompañar. Es un paso decisivo para adaptar nuestros lazos comerciales a las realidades del siglo XX. Y lo es porque elimina casi la totalidad de los aranceles que teníamos hasta ahora y porque actualiza los mecanismos de protección de inversiones al dar más certidumbre a operadores europeos y mexicanos.

Estos son elementos clave que facilitarán las operaciones de las más de 45 000 empresas europeas —muchas de ellas pymes— que exportan a México.

También se trata de un Acuerdo relevante para el acceso a minerales críticos como la fluorita o el cobre, un ámbito donde tenemos que asegurar que no se repitan las dinámicas extractivistas del pasado.

Pero lo importante de este Acuerdo no solo está en lo técnico. El nuevo marco incluye obligaciones vinculantes en materia ambiental, laboral y social. El Acuerdo garantiza el respeto al Acuerdo de París y, además, México ratifica nuevas convenciones de la Organización Internacional del Trabajo, un compromiso que tiene que incluirse como parte esencial del Acuerdo durante la próxima revisión.

En este camino, este Acuerdo tiene que ser un instrumento que contribuya a guiar la inversión hacia sectores de alto valor añadido en México, que diversifique la inversión europea en el país y que logre beneficiar a aquellos que tantas veces quedan atrás, que se convierta en un marco en el que la voz de la sociedad civil y las comunidades indígenas mexicanas sea escuchada y que asegure que sus prioridades no quedan de lado.

En definitiva, dando luz a este Acuerdo, el Parlamento Europeo deja claro que Europa apuesta por la cooperación con socios tan relevantes como México de la mano y sin paternalismos.

Es importante que desde este Parlamento se proyecte determinación en la cooperación con liderazgo, con una Europa que no debe quedarse atrás, que apuesta por su autonomía estratégica, y en un contexto en el que otros levantan barreras.
2-0222-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Commissioner, this Parliament is about to give its consent to an Agreement that has taken almost ten years to negotiate. An Agreement that arrives at a time when global trade can no longer be understood solely in economic terms.

Today, the European Union is more aware than ever that trade policy is a fundamental pillar for our economic security and strategic autonomy. We are aware of the need to diversify our trade relations and strengthen alliances with partners who share our commitment to multilateralism and rules-based global trade.

Mexico is undoubtedly one of the best examples of that kind of strategic ally. Therefore, the signing of the Modernized Global Agreement between the European Union and Mexico is fantastic news that this Parliament must support. It is a decisive step to adapt our trade ties to the realities of the 20th [sic] century. And it is so because it eliminates almost all the tariffs we have had until now and because it updates investment protection mechanisms by giving more certainty to European and Mexican operators.

These are key elements that will facilitate the operations of the more than 45,000 European companies — many of them SMEs — that export to Mexico.

It is also a relevant Agreement for access to critical minerals such as fluorite or copper, an area where we must ensure that the extractivist dynamics of the past are not repeated.

But the importance of this Agreement is not only technical. The new framework includes binding obligations on environmental, labor, and social matters. The Agreement guarantees respect for the Paris Agreement and, furthermore, Mexico ratifies new International Labour Organization conventions, a commitment that must be included as an essential part of the Agreement during the next review.

Along this path, this Agreement must be an instrument that helps guide investment toward high value-added sectors in Mexico, that diversifies European investment in the country and manages to benefit those who are so often left behind, that becomes a framework in which the voice of civil society and Mexican indigenous communities is heard and ensures that their priorities are not sidelined.

In short, by giving the green light to this Agreement, the European Parliament makes it clear that Europe is committed to cooperation with partners as relevant as Mexico, hand in hand and without paternalism.

It is important that this Parliament projects determination in cooperation with leadership, with a Europe that must not lag behind, that is committed to its strategic autonomy, and in a context where others are raising barriers.

Teie ees olevad lepped loovad täiendavaid võimalusi Euroopa ettevõtetele ja majandusele tervikuna. Tollipiirangud ja tariifid vähenevad veelgi ning turud avanevad vastastikku rohkem. Euroopa Liidu ettevõtetel tekib märksa parem ligipääs Mehhiko turule.

Meie suhetes on oluline tähelepanu ka inimõiguste ja õigusriigi põhimõtete järgimisel. Nii on ette nähtud Euroopa Liidu ja Mehhiko dialoog ajakirjanike ja inimõiguste kaitsjate turvalisuse parandamiseks. Kavas on ühised tegevused korruptsiooni, rahapesu ja organiseeritud kuritegevusega võitlemiseks. On ka äärmiselt oluline, et Euroopa Liit on aktiivne ja jätkab sellelaadsete lepingute sõlmimist ka teiste meile potentsiaalselt lähedaste riikidega, et suurendada Euroopa Liidu positiivset mõju maailma arengutes.
2-0224-0000.englishText:
Honored President of the sitting! Dear colleagues! Mexico, with a population of one hundred and thirty-three million, is a strategic partner of the European Union and its second largest trading partner in Latin America. Therefore, relations between the European Union and Mexico have already been very important. At the same time, there is still untapped potential. Therefore, the approval of the agreements deepening EU-Mexico relations before Parliament is important both in our bilateral relations and globally. Considering that the international legal order is under severe pressure, a new agreement based on and strengthening international law is very necessary, and the European Union has an important role to play in this. Relations between states must not be determined by the unilateral power politics of some regime, but by agreements based on international law. The agreements before you create additional opportunities for European businesses and the economy as a whole. Customs restrictions and tariffs will be further reduced and markets will be mutually more open. European Union companies will gain significantly better access to the Mexican market.

Attention to the observance of human rights and the rule of law is also important in our relations. Thus, a dialogue between the European Union and Mexico is envisaged to improve the safety of journalists and human rights defenders. Joint activities are planned to combat corruption, money laundering, and organized crime. It is also extremely important that the European Union is active and continues to conclude similar agreements with other countries potentially close to us, in order to increase the positive impact of the European Union on global developments.

2-0225-0000.sourceText:
Herr Präsident, sehr geehrter Herr Kommissar, liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen! Morgen stimmen wir über die Modernisierung des Mexiko‑Handelsabkommens ab. Ich werde zustimmen, aber habe trotzdem Kritik am Abkommen.

Ja, in einer Welt, in der Donald Trump im Weißen Haus eine erratische Handelspolitik betreibt und China mit unfairen Regeln spielt, brauchen wir Partner. Und ja, Mexiko unter Präsidentin Sheinbaum ist eine solche verlässliche Partnerin – eine Regierung, die für Multilateralismus, Demokratie, soziale Gerechtigkeit und entschlossenen Klimaschutz eintritt, Werte, die momentan wichtiger sind denn je.

Ich begrüße ausdrücklich die engere Kooperation mit Mexiko. Ich befürworte auch die Verbesserungen, die die Modernisierung in den Bereichen Nachhaltigkeit, Korruptionsbekämpfung, Gender usw. mit sich bringt.

Aber zur Wahrheit gehört auch, dass dieses Abkommen weit weg von einem perfekten Abkommen ist. Es gibt kein einklagbares Nachhaltigkeitskapitel wie mit Neuseeland, was Klima-, Umwelt- und Arbeitsstandards am Ende leider zahnlos macht.

Und noch schlimmer: Dieses Abkommen erfüllt beim Investitionsschutz nicht die Forderungen dieses Parlaments. Die veralteten Klauseln verleihen Investoren unverhältnismäßig große Macht und die Möglichkeit, vor internationalen Schiedsgerichten gegen jegliche demokratische Entscheidung vorzugehen, sei es im Klimaschutz oder auch die Versorgung von Medikamenten, bei allen möglichen Themen. Es gibt so krasse Fälle, wo Investoren Staaten verklagen, und ich verstehe nicht, dass die Europäische Union diesen Mechanismus immer noch weiter perpetuiert.

Mitten in der Klimakrise, nachdem eine Hitzewelle in Europa gerade tausenden Menschen das Leben gekostet hat, schafft es die Kommission immer noch nicht, Handelspolitik und Klimaschutz zusammenzudenken. Das muss sich endlich ändern!

Ich erwarte, dass die Kommission bei dem Überprüfungsmechanismus, der bereits in einem Jahr ansteht, diese Zeit nutzt, um endlich Umwelt-, Arbeits- und Klimarechte zu stärken und den Investitionsschutz endlich an unsere demokratischen Werte anzupassen.
2-0225-0000.englishText:
Mr President, dear Commissioner, dear colleagues! Tomorrow we will vote on the modernization of the EU-Mexico trade agreement. I will vote in favor, but nevertheless have criticism of the agreement.

Yes, in a world where Donald Trump pursues erratic trade policy in the White House and China plays by unfair rules, we need partners. And yes, Mexico under President Sheinbaum is such a reliable partner – a government that stands up for multilateralism, democracy, social justice, and decisive climate action, values that are more important than ever at the moment.

I explicitly welcome the closer cooperation with Mexico. I also support the improvements that the modernization brings in the areas of sustainability, anti-corruption, gender, etc.

But the truth also includes the fact that this agreement is far from a perfect agreement. There is no enforceable sustainability chapter like the one with New Zealand, which ultimately leaves climate, environmental, and labor standards toothless.

And even worse: in terms of investment protection, this agreement does not meet the demands of this Parliament. The outdated clauses grant investors disproportionately great power and the opportunity to take action before international arbitration tribunals against any democratic decision, be it in climate protection or even the supply of medicines, on all sorts of issues. There are such glaring cases where investors sue states, and I do not understand that the European Union still continues to perpetuate this mechanism.

In the middle of the climate crisis, after a heatwave in Europe has just cost thousands of people their lives, the Commission still fails to think trade policy and climate protection together. That finally has to change!

I expect the Commission, with the review mechanism that is already due in one year, to use this time to finally strengthen environmental, labor, and climate rights and to finally adapt investment protection to our democratic values.

2-0226-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, I will start by saying that we stand alongside The Left's historical criticism of the trade agreements that the European Union and some other international actors or states have entered into.

Most of the time, these agreements are driven by Eurocentrism and extractivism, and negotiations are not held on equal terms. Huge harm on our first sector and better conditions for industrial production offshoring have been commonplace so far as regards to this trade agreement.

This time, the modernisation of the EU-Mexico trade agreement comes with some considerations that will bring my delegation not to take a stand against it. First of all, we as a Basque political force are very aware of our country's presence in Mexico and therefore protection of the employment in the Basque Country is linked to that.

Secondly, unlike in the case of Mercosur, the impact of Mexican exporters on our economy will not be a significant one as tariffs are not changing this time.

A third point for us is geopolitical solidarity with Mexico. Mexican exports are largely dependent on the USA – over 83 % of the Mexican exports' destiny is the northern neighbour, and Europe should help Mexico in reducing those figures and, by the way, fighting the impact of European corporate activity in the direction against human and environmental rights as well.

Acting this way, we are helping Mexico counteract the effects of Trump's geopolitical greed on the country. And this time, we can show that international solidarity goes beyond speeches.

2-0227-0000.sourceText:
Herr Präsident! Sie reden hier viel über die Probleme in anderen Teilen der Welt, nur über die Probleme in Europa sprechen Sie nicht so gerne. Heute geht es um die Partnerschaft mit Mexiko: finden wir grundsätzlich wichtig – wichtiger Handelspartner.

Nur, leider beschränkt sich der Bericht nicht auf die Handelspolitik. EVP und Sozialisten zeigen sich besorgt über den Zustand der Demokratie in Mexiko. Sie ermahnen die Mexikaner, dass es wichtig sei, ein pluralistisches, demokratisches Umfeld zu erhalten, durch eine angemessene öffentliche Finanzierung politischer Parteien. Aber das, was Sie den Amerikanern vorschreiben wollen, lassen Sie für uns Europäer nicht gelten.

Erst vor wenigen Minuten haben Sie hier einen Verbotsantrag gegen unsere Partei beschlossen. Uns wollen Sie die Gelder streichen, den Mexikanern erklären Sie, dass die öffentliche Finanzierung von Parteien notwendig sei, sonst sei die Demokratie in Gefahr. Was für eine Doppelmoral!

Dann freuen Sie sich noch, dass in Mexiko die Armutsquote gesunken ist und die Renten gestiegen sind. Ist ja schön, nur in Deutschland ist es umgekehrt; da steigt die Armutsquote, und das Rentenniveau sinkt. Jeder fünfte Deutsche ist von Armut bedroht, 7 Millionen Rentner bekommen weniger als 1 000 EUR im Monat.

Statt die mexikanische Regierung für ihre Erfolge bei der Armutsbekämpfung zu loben, sollten wir die deutsche Regierung kritisieren, die immer mehr Menschen in Armut stürzt. Und genau das tun wir; deshalb sind wir erfolgreich. Unsere Partei, die Alternative für Deutschland, ist mit weitem Abstand stärkste Kraft in Deutschland. Sie können uns hier unsere Gelder streichen, aber wir werden trotzdem gewinnen, weil wir die Interessen unserer Bürger vertreten und nicht den Rest der Welt belehren wollen.
2-0227-0000.englishText:
Mr President! You talk a lot here about the problems in other parts of the world, but you do not like talking quite as much about the problems in Europe. Today is about the partnership with Mexico: we consider it fundamentally important – an important trading partner.

Only, unfortunately, the report is not restricted to trade policy. EPP and Socialists express concern about the state of democracy in Mexico. They admonish the Mexicans that it is important to maintain a pluralistic, democratic environment through appropriate public funding of political parties. But what you want to dictate to the Americans, you do not apply to us Europeans.

Just a few minutes ago, you passed a motion to ban our party here. You want to cut our funding, while you explain to the Mexicans that public funding of parties is necessary, otherwise democracy is in danger. What double standards!

Then you are also pleased that the poverty rate in Mexico has fallen and pensions have risen. That is all very well, but in Germany it is the other way round; there the poverty rate is rising, and the pension level is falling. One in five Germans is at risk of poverty, 7 million pensioners receive less than EUR 1,000 a month.

Instead of praising the Mexican government for its successes in combating poverty, we should criticise the German government, which is plunging more and more people into poverty. And that is exactly what we are doing; that is why we are successful. Our party, Alternative for Germany, is by far the strongest force in Germany. You can cut our funding here, but we will win anyway because we represent the interests of our citizens and do not want to lecture the rest of the world.

2-0229-0000.sourceText:
Señora presidenta, la Unión Europea necesita fortalecer sus alianzas con socios estratégicos. Y México, por supuesto, lo es. No solo por el peso de nuestra relación económica, sino porque compartimos una historia, unos intereses comunes y una responsabilidad de defender un orden internacional basado en normas.

Pero precisamente porque aspiramos a una alianza duradera, no podemos conformarnos con hablar únicamente de comercio. Las alianzas estratégicas no se sostienen solo sobre intercambios económicos, se sostienen sobre valores compartidos. Si queremos que este Acuerdo resista el paso del tiempo, debemos ser capaces de exigirnos mutuamente aquello que ambos hemos decidido defender: seguridad jurídica, Estado de Derecho, instituciones sólidas, independencia judicial, protección de las libertades y pleno respeto a los principios democráticos.

La confianza entre socios no nace del silencio, nace de la sinceridad y de la exigencia recíproca. Y eso es lo que hemos comprobado con México. Los Gobiernos negocian los acuerdos, pero son los Parlamentos quienes dan la legitimidad democrática y quienes garantizan su continuidad cuando cambian las mayorías. Por eso, como presidente de la Comisión Parlamentaria Mixta UE-México, quiero dar las gracias a los dos ponentes —Javi López y Borja Jiménez Larraz— por el magnífico trabajo en los informes, al embajador de México —Rogelio Granguillhome— y al embajador europeo —Francisco André—, porque han ayudado a que también el Parlamento Europeo esté representado por primera vez en una firma de un acuerdo. Muchísimas gracias por ello también a sus jefes en la Comisión y en el Consejo —importante—.
2-0229-0000.englishText:
Madam President, the European Union needs to strengthen its alliances with strategic partners. And Mexico, of course, is one. Not only because of the weight of our economic relationship, but because we share a history, common interests and a responsibility to defend a rules-based international order.

But precisely because we aspire to a lasting alliance, we cannot be content with talking solely about trade. Strategic alliances are not sustained solely on economic exchanges, they are sustained on shared values. If we want this Agreement to stand the test of time, we must be capable of demanding of one another what we have both decided to defend: legal certainty, the Rule of Law, solid institutions, judicial independence, the protection of freedoms and full respect for democratic principles.

Trust between partners is not born of silence, it is born of sincerity and reciprocal demand. And that is what we have seen with Mexico. Governments negotiate agreements, but it is Parliaments that provide democratic legitimacy and guarantee their continuity when majorities change. Therefore, as Chair of the EU-Mexico Joint Parliamentary Committee, I want to thank the two rapporteurs —Javi López and Borja Jiménez Larraz— for their magnificent work on the reports, the Ambassador of Mexico —Rogelio Granguillhome— and the European Ambassador —Francisco André—, because they have helped ensure that the European Parliament is also represented for the first time at the signing of an agreement. Thank you very much for that also to their bosses in the Commission and the Council —important—.

2-0230-0000.sourceText:
Frau Präsidentin, Herr Kommissar, liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen! Global leben wir in wirtschaftlich turbulenten Zeiten; das Wasser ist stürmisch. Und das erlebt Mexiko natürlich auch sehr, sehr stark. Herr Trump hat im letzten Jahr achtmal mit verschiedenen Zolldrohungen und Maßnahmen Mexikos Wirtschaft negativ beeinflusst. Es gab Streit über die Wasserverteilung. Wie kann man das heutzutage machen? Es gab andere Druckmittel, sodass die Wirtschaft in Mexiko stagniert.

Mit dem Abkommen erwarten wir eine deutliche Erholung der Wirtschaft in Mexiko, bis zu 35 %. Das ist, glaube ich, genau das, was wir im Moment brauchen – eine Solidarität in der wirtschaftlichen Beziehung und in der Investitionspolitik, sodass Menschen vor Ort die Perspektive auf ein gutes Leben haben.

Deswegen ist es gut, dass wir dieses Abkommen nach vorne bringen; das ist ein Zeichen der Solidarität von uns mit Mexiko. Let's build bridges over troubled water.
2-0230-0000.englishText:
Madam President, dear Commissioner, dear colleagues! Globally, we are living in economically turbulent times; the waters are rough. And of course, Mexico is experiencing this very, very strongly as well. Last year, Mr. Trump negatively impacted Mexico's economy eight times with various tariff threats and measures. There was a dispute over water distribution. How can one do that nowadays? There were other means of pressure, so that the economy in Mexico is stagnating.

With the agreement, we expect a significant recovery of the economy in Mexico, of up to 35%. That is, I believe, exactly what we need at the moment – solidarity in the economic relationship and in investment policy, so that people on the ground have the prospect of a good life.

That is why it is good that we are moving this agreement forward; that is a sign of our solidarity with Mexico. Let's build bridges over troubled water.

2-0231-0000.sourceText:
Madam President, if you allow me just a short intervention, just to react on the first round of speakers. I think Mr Lange just reminded us what kind of turbulent times we are living in right now and why in these times, especially in this period, we need close partnerships with our like-minded partners and also strong solidarity. I think this agreement is a kind of reflection and embodiment of these key ingredients, which have been part and parcel of our negotiations. Ms Pedro already highlighted that already today we have 45 000 European companies that are exporting to Mexico. And what is also very important is the fact that, as she said, and I confirm the figure, more than 80 % of these companies are SMEs. So for small and medium-sized enterprises to trade with a distant partner, it requires simplicity, it has to be smooth, you have to have a good legal and trade framework in place. And I believe that with the modernisation of this agreement, we are clearly delivering on this goal and therefore I believe that we will have more SMEs and more companies investing and cooperating with Mexico.

Ms Jalloul Muro was highlighting that this agreement goes beyond traditional trade issues. She was underscoring the importance of economic security, strategic economy, strategic autonomy, but also the diversification opportunity this agreement offers to Mexico, but also to the European Union. And I think that once we enter into this new partnership with Mexico, it would help us to also address the issues that have been mentioned by Ms Pedro and Ms Cavazzini as true partners who are ready to cooperate together very closely on all issues.

Mr Polato and Mr Barrena Arza, thank you very much for highlighting the complementarity of our economies because especially the topics which are very often passionately discussed also in this chamber, linked to agriculture and the agrifood business, in this particular case, what we have focused on is making sure that our agrifood exports to Mexico will be done with zero duties. And all this would apply to almost all of the EU's key export interests, either at entry into force or within 7 to 10 years. And I have to underscore that this agreement will remove 99 % of the currently very high Mexican tariffs, like 100 % on poultry, 45 % on cheese, 45 % on pork, 20 % on chocolate and pasta, for example. Despite these tariffs, already in 2025, EU agrifood exports are worth EUR 2.3 billion. So I believe that when it comes to the reduction of tariffs, as I just described only for the agrifood business, we are reducing tariffs for European exporters by more than EUR 100 million. So I am absolutely convinced that, also in this sector, it would be extremely beneficial for our agrifood sectors to have such valuable partners as Mexico.

2-0232-0000.sourceText:
Tisztelt Elnök Asszony! Az EU–Mexikó globális megállapodás kétségtelenül új lehetőségeket nyit mindkét fél számára: reméljük, új munkahelyeket és exportpiacokat – javítva a versenyképességünket. A tisztánlátás végett azonban két dolog. Az első: kérem a Bizottságot, sürgősen frissítse az összes szabadkereskedelmi megállapodás együttes hatását vizsgáló 24-es hatástanulmányát a mezőgazdaságra, hogy lássuk, pontosan mivel szembesülnek a gazdáink. Szenteljen különös figyelmet a mézpiacnak. Az ukrán import hatását pedig ezúttal legyen szíves, ne felejtse ki a számításból.

A másik: Ennek a megállapodásnak tagadhatatlanul van politikai vetülete, és az időközi jelentés hemzseg a baloldalnak tett elvtelen engedményektől. Pedig a szerző pontosan tudja: ami a mexikói jogállamisággal történik, az vállalhatatlan. A baloldal ideológiai harcostársainak bűne fölött Brüsszel mindig szemet huny. Scheinbaum Mexikóban, Magyar Péter Magyarországon veri szét a demokratikus rendszert, a Bizottság pedig mélyen hallgat. Önök ezzel a kettős mércével nemcsak ellehetetlenítik, de tönkre is teszik az Uniót, a kölcsönös bizalmat és az együttműködést.
2-0232-0000.englishText:
Madam President! The EU-Mexico Global Agreement undoubtedly opens up new opportunities for both parties: hopefully new jobs and export markets - improving our competitiveness. For the sake of clarity, however, two things. First: I ask the Commission to urgently update its 2024 impact assessment examining the combined effect of all free trade agreements on agriculture, so that we can see exactly what our farmers are facing. Pay special attention to the honey market. And please do not leave the impact of Ukrainian imports out of the calculation this time.

The other: This agreement undeniably has a political dimension, and the interim report teems with principled concessions made to the left. Yet the author knows full well: what is happening to the rule of law in Mexico is unacceptable. Brussels always turns a blind eye to the sins of the ideological comrades-in-arms of the left. Scheinbaum in Mexico, Péter Magyar in Hungary are smashing the democratic order, and the Commission remains deeply silent. With this double standard, you are not only making the Union impossible, but you are destroying it, along with mutual trust and cooperation.
2-0232-0000.factCheck: The claim that Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar is an "ideological comrade-in-arms of the left" who is "smashing the democratic order" is false, as his Tisza Party is a centre-right, pro-European party affiliated with the European People's Party, and he was democratically elected in April 2026 on a platform of restoring the rule of law after 16 years of Fidesz rule.

2-0233-0000.sourceText:
Pani Przewodnicząca! Panie Komisarzu! Czy wy nie nauczyliście się jeszcze wyciągać wniosków z historii? To, co działo się we współpracy z Chinami, powinno pokazywać, w którym kierunku należy iść. Wiele lat temu dokładnie takie same nadzieje pokładano w handlu z Chinami jak dzisiaj z Mercosurem, z Indiami, teraz z Meksykiem. Do niczego dobrego to nie doprowadziło. Dzisiaj mamy czasy, w których powinniśmy budować odporność, niezależność, ponieważ geopolityka jest dzisiaj taka, że drobny konflikt na świecie powoduje dramatyczne konsekwencje.

A my idziemy cały czas w procesie uzależniania się od handlu zagranicznego z krajami bardzo odległymi od Unii Europejskiej. To jest zły kierunek. COVID i inne wojny na Bliskim Wschodzie pokazały, że to jest bardzo zły kierunek, ale nie wyciągamy z tego żadnych wniosków. Problem polega na tym, że kiedy Niemcy podejmowali głupie decyzje, szkodzili sami sobie i niszczyli własną gospodarkę właśnie poprzez handel gazem z Rosją, poprzez likwidowanie energii atomowej, poprzez handel z Chinami. To była ich sprawa. A dzisiaj problem polega na tym, że mają wpływ na całą Unię Europejską i te głupoty każą stosować i w nich uczestniczyć wszystkim członkom. I to jest największy problem dzisiejszej sytuacji.
2-0233-0000.englishText:
Madam President! Commissioner! Have you not yet learned to draw conclusions from history? What happened in cooperation with China should show the direction in which we must go. Many years ago, exactly the same hopes were placed in trade with China as today with Mercosur, with India, and now with Mexico. It has led to nothing good. Today we are in times when we should build resilience and independence, because geopolitics today is such that a minor conflict anywhere in the world causes dramatic consequences.

And we are constantly continuing the process of becoming dependent on foreign trade with countries very distant from the European Union. This is the wrong direction. COVID and other wars in the Middle East have shown that this is a very bad direction, but we are not drawing any conclusions from it. The problem is that when Germany made foolish decisions, they harmed themselves and destroyed their own economy precisely through gas trade with Russia, through phasing out nuclear energy, and through trade with China. That was their own affair. And today the problem is that they have an influence on the entire European Union and they force all members to apply this nonsense and participate in it. And that is the biggest problem of today's situation.

2-0234-0000.sourceText:
Senhora Presidente, Senhor Comissário Šefčovič, nesta altura em que parece mais fácil lançar tarifas, que são uma espécie de muros, dá particular gozo falar aqui de acordos comerciais, que são uma espécie de pontes. E esta modernização do acordo global com o México e o acordo comercial interino são uma bela ponte.

Não são só os 99 % de tarifas que desaparecem, que só no agroalimentar representam mais de 100 mil milhões de EUR de poupanças para os exportadores europeus, mas são também todos os outros impactos que este mercado vai ter, nomeadamente o facto de nos abrir 130 milhões de consumidores mexicanos, e fará com que as nossas trocas comerciais cresçam rapidamente, ultrapassarão os 100 mil milhões de EUR muito rapidamente.

Também clarifica as regras de acesso ao mercado digital e torna mais fácil o acesso dos europeus a matérias primas críticas.

Gostávamos que essa ponte tivesse mais um troço. Sim, gostávamos que tivesse o capítulo da energia e é nossa responsabilidade fazê-lo antes do fim do primeiro período de revisão deste acordo.

Mas também tem troços perfeitamente novos: o acesso a concursos públicos por parte de empresas europeias, nomeadamente em concursos públicos de nível estadual, e a inovadora cláusula de combate e prevenção da corrupção, porque não há comércio livre sem instituições livres e transparentes, fazendo fé daquilo que realmente é o primeiro passo para o combate à corrupção, que é o combate, também, à burocracia.

Portanto, pedimos, caros colegas, que aprovem este acordo quando vier à votação, porque acreditamos na força do comércio livre, acreditamos porque o comércio livre tirou centenas de milhões de pessoas da miséria nas últimas décadas e acreditamos que lutar por um comércio mais livre é lutar por uma Europa mais forte.
2-0234-0000.englishText:
Madam President, Commissioner Šefčovič, at a time when it seems easier to launch tariffs, which are a kind of walls, it is particularly enjoyable to speak here about trade agreements, which are a kind of bridges. And this modernisation of the global agreement with Mexico and the interim trade agreement are a fine bridge.

It is not only the 99% of tariffs that disappear, which in the agri-food sector alone represent more than EUR 100 billion in savings for European exporters, but it is also all the other impacts that this market will have, namely the fact that it opens up 130 million Mexican consumers to us, and will make our trade grow rapidly, exceeding EUR 100 billion very quickly.

It also clarifies the rules for access to the digital market and makes it easier for Europeans to access critical raw materials.

We would like this bridge to have one more section. Yes, we would like it to have the energy chapter and it is our responsibility to do so before the end of the first review period of this agreement.

But it also has completely new sections: access to public procurement by European companies, namely in state-level public procurement, and the innovative clause to combat and prevent corruption, because there is no free trade without free and transparent institutions, relying on what is truly the first step in the fight against corruption, which is also the fight against bureaucracy.

Therefore, we ask you, dear colleagues, to approve this agreement when it comes to a vote, because we believe in the power of free trade, we believe because free trade has lifted hundreds of millions of people out of poverty in recent decades and we believe that fighting for freer trade is fighting for a stronger Europe.

2-0235-0000.sourceText:
Señora presidenta, señor comisario, la Unión Europea debe buscar nuevas alianzas, de todo tipo: comerciales, políticas e incluso seguramente de defensa. El viejo mundo que conocíamos está agonizando y la Unión Europea debe hacerse un lugar en el nuevo mundo que está naciendo. Alianzas con países hermanos como México son claves. Son una oportunidad geopolítica de primer orden. Aquí, todos estamos de acuerdo; en lo que quizás ya no estamos todos de acuerdo es con qué herramientas construimos estas alianzas.

Para nosotros, un tipo de acuerdo que sí contempla medidas sancionadoras vinculantes en caso de no respetar el acuerdo comercial, pero que solo plantea meras recomendaciones cuando se vulneran los derechos humanos o medioambientales no ayuda a construir el mundo que queremos.

Pero es que además, en el ámbito comercial, son acuerdos que no responden a todos los intereses que necesitamos en Europa. Fíjense, por ejemplo, en la industria del automóvil. En los últimos meses, hemos visto cómo Audi cerraba definitivamente su planta en Bruselas y destruía 3 000 empleos directos. Mientras tanto, se consolida el traslado de la producción de modelos históricos como el Volkswagen Golf a la planta de Puebla, en México, lo que deja vacías las líneas de montaje en Alemania. ¿Esto es un buen acuerdo? Para la cuenta de resultados de las multinacionales, sí, pero para las familias trabajadoras evidentemente no. Y esto es solo la punta del iceberg.

La pregunta no es si queremos una alianza con México: la queremos. La pregunta es si estamos dispuestos a construirlo sobre estos cimientos. Nosotros lo tenemos claro: el progreso de Europa no se defiende destruyendo su industria ni su precarización, el empleo aquí o allá. Por eso, por coherencia y por justicia social, votaremos en contra.
2-0235-0000.englishText:
Madam President, Commissioner, the European Union must seek new alliances of all kinds: commercial, political, and surely even in defense. The old world we knew is dying, and the European Union must carve out a place for itself in the new world that is being born. Alliances with sister countries like Mexico are key. They are a first-rate geopolitical opportunity. Here, we all agree; where we perhaps no longer all agree is with what tools we build these alliances.

For us, a type of agreement that does include binding sanctioning measures in the event of non-compliance with the trade agreement, but only proposes mere recommendations when human rights or environmental rights are violated, does not help to build the world we want.

Furthermore, in the commercial sphere, these are agreements that do not respond to all the interests we need in Europe. Look, for example, at the automotive industry. In recent months, we have seen how Audi definitively closed its plant in Brussels and destroyed 3,000 direct jobs. Meanwhile, the relocation of the production of historic models such as the Volkswagen Golf to the plant in Puebla, in Mexico, is being consolidated, which leaves assembly lines empty in Germany. Is this a good agreement? For the profit and loss statement of multinationals, yes, but for working families, obviously not. And this is just the tip of the iceberg.

Detected language: es
The question is not whether we want an alliance with Mexico: we want it. The question is whether we are willing to build it on these foundations. For us, it is clear: Europe's progress is not defended by destroying its industry or through its precarization, employment here or there. Therefore, out of coherence and social justice, we will vote against it.

2-0236-0000.sourceText:
Madame la Présidente, Monsieur le Commissaire, donner tout le pouvoir aux multinationales, voilà ce que vous vous apprêtez à faire avec ce nouvel accord de libre-échange avec le Mexique. Et il faudrait qu’on soit là à applaudir des deux mains! Les entreprises ne s’y trompent d’ailleurs pas. Attirées par une main-d’œuvre bon marché et des droits de douane réduits à néant, elles en profitent déjà pour délocaliser massivement, comme le groupe Volkswagen qui, en même temps qu’il délocalise l’assemblage de ses voitures Audi et Golf au Mexique, supprime au moins 50 000 emplois en Europe.

Mais le scandale de cet accord ne s’arrête pas là. Demain, des entreprises pourront attaquer l’État mexicain ou les États européens devant une juridiction internationale privée et réclamer plusieurs centaines de millions d’euros si une politique publique ne leur convient pas, par exemple pour garder le contrôle public sur l’énergie ou préserver l’environnement. C’est exactement ce même mécanisme scandaleux qui était présent dans le TAFTA, dans le CETA, dans le traité sur la Charte de l’énergie, dont les Européens ont déjà dit haut et fort qu’ils n’en voulaient pas.

Alors, collègues de gauche, socialistes, écologistes qui vous apprêtez à voter cet accord, comment pouvez-vous accepter cet accord complètement injuste qui va accélérer la désindustrialisation, éroder un peu plus notre souveraineté alimentaire et promouvoir une extraction sans limite de matières premières? Au foot, on appelle ça un tir contre son camp. Monsieur le Commissaire, si vous me le permettez, votre politique du «tout libre-échange» mérite un carton rouge. C’est pourquoi notre groupe de la gauche continuera à se mobiliser contre ce «tout libre-échange» au niveau européen.
2-0236-0000.englishText:
Madam President, Commissioner, giving all the power to multinationals, that is what you are preparing to do with this new free trade agreement with Mexico. And we are supposed to be here applauding with both hands! Companies are certainly not fooled by this. Attracted by cheap labor and zero customs duties, they are already taking advantage of this to massively relocate, like the Volkswagen group which, at the same time as it is relocating the assembly of its Audi and Golf cars to Mexico, is cutting at least 50,000 jobs in Europe.

But the scandal of this agreement does not stop there. Tomorrow, companies will be able to sue the Mexican State or European States before a private international jurisdiction and claim several hundred million euros if a public policy does not suit them, for example to keep public control over energy or preserve the environment. This is the exact same scandalous mechanism that was present in TTIP, in CETA, in the Energy Charter Treaty, which Europeans have already loudly and clearly stated they do not want.

So, left-wing, socialist, and environmentalist colleagues who are preparing to vote for this agreement, how can you accept this completely unjust agreement that will accelerate deindustrialization, further erode our food sovereignty, and promote limitless extraction of raw materials? In soccer, that is called an own goal. Commissioner, if you will allow me, your "all-free-trade" policy deserves a red card. That is why our Left group will continue to mobilize against this "all-free-trade" at the European level.

2-0237-0000.sourceText:
Г-жо Председател, пред нас е споразумение, което ще отвори европейските пазари за безмитен внос на пчелен мед от Мексико в размер, сравним с производството на пчелен мед в три Българии. Първо, квотата се увеличава до 35 000 тона. След седмата година всички ограничения отпадат. Това се случва в момент, когато европейските институции сами предупреждават за риска от фалшифициран мед. Изследване от кошерите на съвместен изследователски център на Европейската комисия показва, че при 22 изследвания на проби мед с произход Мексико, при повече от една четвърт има съмнение за фалшифициране. Става въпрос за фалшив мед, пчелен мед, колеги.

Още по-необяснимо е, че Мексико дори не използва изцяло сегашната си безмитна квота. Защо тогава предлагаме още по-голяма либерализация? Не можем да жертваме европейските пчелари, в замяна на търговски отстъпки в други сектори, защото когато унищожим собственото си производство, губят не само пчеларите, губят и европейските потребители, които имат право на истински, качествен и безплатен мед.
2-0237-0000.englishText:
Madam President, before us is an agreement that will open European markets to duty-free imports of honey from Mexico in an amount comparable to the honey production of three Bulgarias. First, the quota is increased to 35,000 tonnes. After the seventh year, all restrictions are lifted. This is happening at a time when the European institutions themselves are warning about the risk of falsified honey. Research from hives by the Joint Research Centre of the European Commission shows that out of 22 tests of honey samples originating from Mexico, more than a quarter are suspected of being falsified. We are talking about fake honey, honey, colleagues.

Even more inexplicably, Mexico does not even fully use its current duty-free quota. Why then are we offering even greater liberalization? We cannot sacrifice European beekeepers in exchange for trade concessions in other sectors, because when we destroy our own production, not only do the beekeepers lose, but European consumers also lose, as they have the right to real, quality, and [pure/unadulterated - free] honey.

2-0238-0000.sourceText:
Madam President, Commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the modernised global agreement is more than just a trade agreement; it is a comprehensive and strategic renewal of the relationship between Mexico and the European Union. As such, I am sure it will provide an updated framework for political dialogue, economic cooperation and sectoral engagement across a wide range of policy areas.

Against the backdrop of growing geopolitical uncertainty and increasing pressure on the rules-based international order, the agreements with Mexico highlight the European Union's commitment to strengthening cooperation with like-minded partners.

Most of today's challenges are transnational and therefore they require international cooperation. Be it security, migration, digitalisation, energy or climate change, we all know that none of these complex issues can be addressed by any country alone. Consequently, our relations with strategic partners no longer focus solely on trade, but also address the multifaceted concerns of an increasingly connected world. The modernised global agreement is a prime example of exactly this approach; in particular, I welcome the strong and timely political signal it sends in support of openness, fairness and international cooperation with our partners in Latin America and beyond.

2-0239-0000.sourceText:
Signora Presidente, onorevoli colleghi, mentre gli Stati Uniti mettono in discussione l'accordo che lega Stati Uniti, Canada e Messico, e che per trent'anni è stato il pilastro dell'integrazione economica nordamericana, l'Europa fa una scelta opposta e rafforza le proprie alleanze.

L'accordo con il Messico è una scelta geopolitica fondamentale: in un mondo frammentato, diversificare i mercati rafforza la nostra autonomia strategica.

Insieme al Canada, ai paesi del Mercosur, all'Australia e ad altri partner, stiamo lavorando per costruire uno spazio di medie potenze che credono nel commercio aperto e nelle regole, riducendo la dipendenza da attori terzi. E l'Unione europea, come spazio che può essere una grande potenza democratica, può ambire a guidare questo cambiamento.

Una strategia di importanza globale che ha anche benefici, per i nostri territori, molto immediati. Penso alle imprese dei nostri territori, dell'Italia, con indicazioni geografiche protette come quelle per i formaggi o quelle per i vini. Abbiamo prodotti che sono tutelati e che potranno raggiungere con maggiore facilità i consumatori messicani.

Anche questo è un pezzo importante della nostra strategia per il futuro dell'economia della nostra Unione.
2-0239-0000.englishText:
Madam President, honourable members, while the United States is questioning the agreement linking the United States, Canada and Mexico, which for thirty years has been the pillar of North American economic integration, Europe is making the opposite choice and strengthening its alliances.

The agreement with Mexico is a fundamental geopolitical choice: in a fragmented world, diversifying markets strengthens our strategic autonomy.

Together with Canada, the Mercosur countries, Australia and other partners, we are working to build a space of middle powers that believe in open trade and rules, reducing dependence on third-party actors. And the European Union, as a space that can be a great democratic power, can aim to lead this change.

A strategy of global importance that also has very immediate benefits for our regions. I am thinking of businesses in our regions, in Italy, with protected geographical indications such as those for cheeses or those for wines. We have products that are protected and that will be able to reach Mexican consumers more easily.

This too is an important piece of our strategy for the future of our Union's economy.

2-0240-0000.sourceText:
Frau Präsidentin, sehr geehrte Damen und Herren! Dieses Haus wird heute vor vollendete Tatsachen gestellt. Die Kommission hat dieses Abkommen bewusst gesplittet. Das Interims-Handelsabkommen tritt in Kraft, sobald dieses Parlament und der mexikanische Senat zustimmen. Die nationalen Parlamente, der österreichische Nationalrat eingeschlossen, dürfen erst im Nachhinein ratifizieren, wenn längst vollendete Tatsachen geschaffen wurden. Das ist keine Handelspolitik, das ist Demokratieumgehung mit Ansage.

Und während man uns von Wachstum und Diversifizierung erzählt, werden unter dem Deckmantel des Freihandels munter Green Deal-Ideologie und Nachhaltigkeitsziele-Bürokratie in ein Handelsabkommen geschmuggelt, das eigentlich unseren Bauern und unserem Mittelstand dienen sollte, nicht Brüsseler Wunschprojekten. Diesem demokratiepolitisch fragwürdigen Vorgehen können wir unser Vertrauen nicht aussprechen.

Gleichzeitig wissen wir um die berechtigten Interessen jener heimischen Betriebe, die auf faire und verlässliche Marktchancen angewiesen sind. Diesen Widerspruch löst die Kommission mit ihrem Vorgehen nicht; sie hat ihn selbst geschaffen.
2-0240-0000.englishText:
Madam President, ladies and gentlemen! This House is being presented with a fait accompli today. The Commission has deliberately split this agreement. The interim trade agreement will enter into force as soon as this Parliament and the Mexican Senate approve it. The national parliaments, including the Austrian National Council, are only allowed to ratify it afterwards, once facts have long been created on the ground. That is not trade policy, that is premeditated circumvention of democracy.

And while we are being told about growth and diversification, under the guise of free trade, Green Deal ideology and sustainability goals bureaucracy are cheerfully being smuggled into a trade agreement that should actually serve our farmers and our SMEs, not Brussels' pet projects. We cannot place our trust in this procedurally and democratically questionable procedure.

At the same time, we are aware of the legitimate interests of those domestic businesses that depend on fair and reliable market opportunities. The Commission is not resolving this contradiction with its approach; it has created it itself.

2-0241-0000.sourceText:
Voorzitter, commissaris, dit gemoderniseerde akkoord met Mexico komt op een cruciaal moment, en wel om verschillende redenen.

Op geopolitiek vlak versterken we onze positie in Latijns-Amerika en bouwen we een betrouwbaar partnerschap uit in een regio waarin ook andere spelers hun invloed trachten te vergroten.

Op economisch vlak opent dit akkoord bovendien nieuwe kansen voor onze bedrijven, onder meer via een betere toegang tot overheidsopdrachten en minder administratieve lasten.

Het bevestigt ons geloof in vrije, op regels gebaseerde handel in deze moeilijke tijden van deglobalisering en fragmentatie. Bovendien zet het duidelijke stappen vooruit in de verbetering van arbeidsomstandigheden en duurzaamheidsnormen.

Tot slot, mijnheer de commissaris, roep ik u op deze ambitieuze handelsagenda consequent voort te zetten. De EU moet blijven kiezen voor sterke handelsakkoorden die welvaart, veerkracht en een open strategische autonomie verder versterken.
2-0241-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Commissioner, this modernized agreement with Mexico comes at a crucial moment, and for several reasons.

On a geopolitical level, we are strengthening our position in Latin America and building a reliable partnership in a region where other players are also trying to increase their influence.

On an economic level, this agreement also opens up new opportunities for our businesses, including through better access to public procurement and reduced administrative burdens.

It reaffirms our belief in free, rules-based trade in these difficult times of deglobalization and fragmentation. Moreover, it takes clear steps forward in improving working conditions and sustainability standards.

Finally, Commissioner, I call on you to consistently pursue this ambitious trade agenda. The EU must continue to opt for strong trade agreements that further strengthen prosperity, resilience and an open strategic autonomy.

2-0242-0000.sourceText:
Frau Präsidentin! Jedes Mal, wenn wir hier über Freihandel reden, entblößen sich die Kollegen von links mit ihrem ökonomischen Unwissen. Deswegen sage ich das gerne noch mal ganz deutlich: Wirtschaftliche Abhängigkeit treibt uns in die politische Abhängigkeit. Das haben wir beim russischen Gas gesehen; das sehen wir bei kritischen Rohstoffen aus China. Die Lösung kann doch nicht Abschottung sein. Sie heißt mehr Handel mit mehr Partnern, auch wenn Linke das nicht wahrhaben wollen.

Das modernisierte Abkommen mit Mexiko ist ein wichtiger Erfolg für unseren Wohlstand und für Europas strategische Unabhängigkeit. Wohlstand entsteht nicht hinter Zollmauern; Wohlstand entsteht, wenn Menschen miteinander Handel treiben. Mit diesem Abkommen können unsere Exporte nach Mexiko um bis zu 75 % steigen. Europäische Unternehmen können bis zu 100 Millionen Euro an Zöllen sparen. Und wir sichern den Zugang zu kritischen Rohstoffen, schaffen neue Chancen von Mittelstand bis Landwirtschaft und Industrie. So geht strategische Unabhängigkeit, und so geht europäische Stärke, liebe Kollegen!
2-0242-0000.englishText:
Madam President! Every time we talk about free trade here, our colleagues on the left expose their economic ignorance. That is why I am happy to say it again very clearly: economic dependence drives us into political dependence. We saw that with Russian gas; we see it with critical raw materials from China. The solution cannot be isolation. It is called more trade with more partners, even if the left does not want to accept that.

The modernized agreement with Mexico is an important success for our prosperity and for Europe's strategic independence. Prosperity is not created behind tariff walls; prosperity is created when people trade with one another. With this agreement, our exports to Mexico can increase by up to 75%. European companies can save up to 100 million euros in tariffs. And we are securing access to critical raw materials, creating new opportunities from small and medium-sized enterprises to agriculture and industry. This is how strategic independence works, and this is how European strength works, dear colleagues!

2-0243-0000.sourceText:
Voorzitter, collega's, dit beleid van de Europese Commissie is volstrekt onbegrijpelijk. Gisteren hebben we nog gedebatteerd over onze automobielindustrie, die uit Europa vertrokken is en elk jaar duizenden jobs verloren ziet gaan. En wat doet deze Commissie? Zij sluit opnieuw een neoliberaal handelsakkoord, een akkoord dat onze industriële capaciteit ondermijnt en werknemers wereldwijd tegen elkaar zal uitspelen.

Europese autoproducenten zullen hun assemblage nog goedkoper naar Mexico kunnen verplaatsen. Gevolg: opnieuw duizenden jobs weg. Ook geeft het akkoord grote bedrijven het recht om overheden aan te klagen als zij het nog maar durven om een sociaal beleid te voeren dat hun winstmarges zou kunnen hypothekeren.

Ik dacht dat de Europese Unie aan industriepolitiek ging doen, maar wat zien we in plaats daarvan? Opnieuw dezelfde neoliberale recepten die ons in deze crisis hebben gestort. Wat wij nodig hebben, is een eerlijke deal die welvaart creëert voor de EU en voor Mexico, en niet alleen voor multinationals. Stem dit akkoord dus weg.
2-0243-0000.englishText:
Mr President, colleagues, this policy of the European Commission is completely incomprehensible. Yesterday we debated our automotive industry, which has left Europe and sees thousands of jobs lost every year. And what does this Commission do? It is once again concluding a neoliberal trade agreement, an agreement that undermines our industrial capacity and will pit workers worldwide against each other.

European car manufacturers will be able to move their assembly to Mexico even more cheaply. Result: thousands of jobs gone again. The agreement also gives large companies the right to sue governments if they even dare to pursue a social policy that might mortgage their profit margins.

I thought the European Union was going to engage in industrial policy, but what do we see instead? Once again the same neoliberal recipes that plunged us into this crisis. What we need is a fair deal that creates prosperity for the EU and for Mexico, and not just for multinationals. So vote this agreement down.

2-0244-0000.sourceText:
Señora presidenta, México es un socio estratégico de la Unión Europea y —por ende— en estos momentos de fragmentación del orden internacional es necesario reforzar nuestros lazos a través de la modernización del Acuerdo Global y de la aprobación del Acuerdo Comercial Interino.

De esta manera, incrementaremos el comercio reduciendo más los aranceles, abarcando más rubros y protegiendo mejor a los productores. Pero también es necesario profundizar el diálogo político, abrir temas como la independencia judicial y el Estado de Derecho. Y no podemos ignorar el grave problema de los desaparecidos. Cuando estuvimos con EuroLat en México, el número oficial era de 130 000 personas, pero ese número sigue incrementando.

Comparto la preocupación de Amnistía Internacional por los operativos de la Ciudad de México por la represión durante las manifestaciones de los familiares de desaparecidos. Por ello, no debemos callarnos. Hay que apoyar el Acuerdo Global Modernizado, pero también denunciar las derivas autoritarias porque nuestro compromiso y amistad no es con un Gobierno, sino con el hermano y querido pueblo mexicano.
2-0244-0000.englishText:
Madam President, Mexico is a strategic partner of the European Union and therefore, in these times of fragmentation of the international order, it is necessary to reinforce our ties through the modernization of the Global Agreement and the approval of the Interim Trade Agreement.

In this way, we will increase trade by further reducing tariffs, covering more areas and better protecting producers. But it is also necessary to deepen political dialogue, opening up issues such as judicial independence and the Rule of Law. And we cannot ignore the serious problem of the disappeared. When we were with EuroLat in Mexico, the official number was 130 000 people, but that number continues to increase.

I share Amnesty International's concern about the operations in Mexico City regarding the repression during the demonstrations of the families of the disappeared. Therefore, we must not remain silent. We must support the Modernized Global Agreement, but also denounce authoritarian trends because our commitment and friendship is not with a Government, but with the brotherly and beloved Mexican people.

2-0245-0000.sourceText:
Señora presidenta, señor comisario, con nuestro apoyo, Europa y México no solo sellarán un acuerdo estratégico, sino una forma compartida de entender el mundo. Es una alianza entre dos democracias que, frente a quienes usan su poder para imponer su voluntad y su beneficio propio, defienden el diálogo, la cooperación y las reglas claras y pactadas para construir la paz, la prosperidad y el desarrollo sostenible colectivo.

Lo apoyamos porque refuerza el diálogo político con un socio estratégico, porque se basa en la cooperación y beneficia a la salud, la educación y la investigación, también a la preparación contra los desastres, porque respeta a las personas y a los recursos naturales y porque está basado en el compromiso y los derechos humanos, el Acuerdo de París, los derechos laborales, el comercio, la igualdad y el medio ambiente. Porque, además, abre nuevas oportunidades a nuestras pymes y protege especialmente a sectores como el turrón o los cítricos.

Pero, sobre todo, lo apoyamos porque, en el actual tablero geopolítico, un acuerdo con un país como México es la mejor brújula. Desde el respeto mutuo, desde el reconocimiento a nuestra propia historia, a nuestra diversidad y desde la cooperación.
2-0245-0000.englishText:
Madam President, Commissioner, with our support, Europe and Mexico will not only seal a strategic agreement, but a shared way of understanding the world. It is an alliance between two democracies that, in the face of those who use their power to impose their will and their own benefit, defend dialogue, cooperation, and clear, agreed-upon rules to build peace, prosperity, and collective sustainable development.
