Pane předsedající, vážená paní komisařko, zajistit bezpečnost našich obyvatel je jednou z největších priorit, ale zároveň výzev, které v Evropské unii v současné době čelíme. A právě otázka kybernetické bezpečnosti se v dnešním světě stává stále palčivější. Nástup umělé inteligence dělá kybernetické útoky rychlejší, sofistikovanější a nebezpečnější než kdy dříve. Proto vítám akční plán Evropské komise pro kybernetickou bezpečnost a umělou inteligenci. Evropa musí být připravena chránit své občany a své podniky i svou kritickou infrastrukturu.

Současně si ale musíme přiznat jednu nepříjemnou skutečnost. Evropa v posledních letech přijímala jednu regulaci za druhou. Místo toho, abychom vytvářeli prostředí pro inovace, stali jsme se světovým lídrem v psaní pravidel. A výsledkem je prostředí, které přimělo mnoho startupů a inovativních firem přesunout svůj vývoj mimo Evropskou unii. A to opravdu není úspěch. To je spíše varování pro nás všechny. Pokud chceme být opravdu lídrem v oblasti kybernetické bezpečnosti a umělé inteligence, tak nemůžeme pouze regulovat technologie, které se vyvíjí jinde. Musíme vytvořit takové podmínky, aby tyto technologie vznikaly právě v Evropě, a proto bych měl na Komisi několik konkrétních otázek:

Jak tento akční plán zabrání dalšímu odlivu inovací z Evropské unie? Jak zajistí, že posilování kybernetické bezpečnosti nebude znamenat další administrativní zátěž pro evropské podniky, a zejména pro malé a střední firmy? A kde je stejně ambiciózní plán na podporu evropských vývojářů, startupů a technologických firem? Protože bez nich nebude Evropa nikdy technologicky soběstačná, ale bude jen regulovat technologie vyvinuté někde jinde. Jak Komise zajistí, aby citlivé bezpečnostní údaje zůstaly pod evropskou kontrolou a neopouštěly Evropskou unii? A závěrem. Podle jakých kritérií a ukazatelů bude Komise měřit úspěch tohoto akčního plánu?

Při projednávání nových pravidel kybernetické bezpečnosti máme příležitost poučit se z minulosti. Potřebujeme taková řešení, která zvýší bezpečnost, ale zároveň podpoří evropské inovace, investice a výzkum. Bezpečnost a konkurenceschopnost totiž nejsou protiklady a jedna bez druhé nemůže existovat. Bez evropských inovací totiž Evropa nebude bezpečná a suverénní.
2-0293-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Commissioner, ensuring the security of our citizens is one of the greatest priorities, but also challenges, that we currently face in the European Union. And the issue of cybersecurity is becoming increasingly pressing in today's world. The advent of artificial intelligence is making cyber attacks faster, more sophisticated and more dangerous than ever before. Therefore, I welcome the European Commission's action plan for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Europe must be prepared to protect its citizens, its businesses and its critical infrastructure.

At the same time, however, we must admit one unpleasant reality. In recent years, Europe has adopted one regulation after another. Instead of creating an environment for innovation, we have become a global leader in rule-making. And the result is an environment that has led many startups and innovative companies to move their development outside the European Union. And that is really not a success. That is rather a warning to all of us. If we truly want to be a leader in the field of cybersecurity and artificial intelligence, we cannot simply regulate technologies that are developed elsewhere. We must create conditions such that these technologies are created right in Europe, and therefore I have several specific questions for the Commission:

How will this action plan prevent the further outflow of innovation from the European Union? How will it ensure that strengthening cybersecurity will not mean additional administrative burdens for European businesses, and especially for small and medium-sized enterprises? And where is an equally ambitious plan to support European developers, startups and technology companies? Because without them, Europe will never be technologically self-sufficient, but will only regulate technologies developed elsewhere. How will the Commission ensure that sensitive security data remains under European control and does not leave the European Union? And in conclusion, according to what criteria and indicators will the Commission measure the success of this action plan?

When discussing new cybersecurity rules, we have the opportunity to learn from the past. We need solutions that will increase security while supporting European innovation, investment and research. Security and competitiveness are not opposites and one cannot exist without the other. Without European innovation, Europe will not be secure and sovereign.

2-0294-0000.sourceText:
Panie Przewodniczący! Ta debata nie jest o cyberbezpieczeństwie i o sztucznej inteligencji. Ta debata jest dowodem klęski Unii Europejskiej w ciągu ostatnich 20-30 lat.

Europa niegdyś była kontynentem, gdzie dokonywano największych technicznych odkryć. Była kontynentem, gdzie odbywała się rewolucja przemysłowa. Była kontynentem, który dyktował rozwój praktycznie całego świata.

Dzisiaj jesteśmy wspólnotą, która ze swoich podatków dotuje biurokrację, która nie wnosi nic innowacyjnego ani nic nowoczesnego. Jedziemy wagonem drugiej klasy. Na naszych oczach odbywa się absolutna rewolucja, porównywalna z wprowadzeniem komputerów. Wpłynie ona na gospodarkę, na społeczeństwa, na każdy aspekt naszego życia. A my siedzimy w drugiej klasie, dlatego że biurokracja, regulacje i brak innowacyjności to motto dzisiejszej europejskiej biurokracji.
2-0294-0000.englishText:
Mr President! This debate is not about cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. This debate is proof of the European Union's failure over the last 20-30 years.

Europe was once a continent where the greatest technical discoveries were made. It was a continent where the industrial revolution took place. It was a continent that dictated the development of practically the entire world.

Today, we are a community that subsidizes bureaucracy from its taxes, which contributes nothing innovative or modern. We are riding in a second-class carriage. An absolute revolution, comparable to the introduction of computers, is taking place before our eyes. It will affect the economy, societies, and every aspect of our lives. And we are sitting in second class because bureaucracy, regulations, and a lack of innovation are the motto of today's European bureaucracy.

2-0295-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, I call on all business leaders in Europe to take good note of today's recommendations on AI and cybersecurity, released by the European Commission and ENISA.

It is not business as usual anymore. Your software and IT systems will be tested by hackers. Aided by the latest AI models, hackers will operate at the speed of light, and will try to put you out of business. So, today's recommendations will help you to defend at the speed of light, and with the help of the best talent and the best capabilities Europe has to offer.

I also remind business leaders that time is not to your advantage. You have a few months, at best, to fix vulnerabilities, because AI models from China with similar capabilities will be on the market soon. You must adapt to stay in business.

But I also want to encourage my colleagues here to think firmly about developing frontier AI models in Europe. Currently, there are some 3 000 large language models in the world, only 30 of which are European. Zero are compliant with EU laws and regulations. So, if we want sovereign European technology, we need to push for deregulation – indeed, at the speed of light.

2-0296-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, colleagues, Commissioner, for months, some of us have been warning that Europe was sleepwalking into a new dependency, and restrictions on Mythos, Fable and now GPT-5.6 proved the point better than any speech here.

Everything here in this new action plan is guidelines, blueprints and pilots. It is a necessary start to this problem, yes. But where is the joint procurement as a collective leverage? Where is the economic and diplomatic pressure to make sure Europe is not, again, cut off? Nothing binds the plan to CSA2. No appeal mechanism is proposed. I ask 'why?'

Most importantly, we need to focus on creating the industrial foundation for Europe to compete globally with our own cutting-edge models. That means sovereign compute, increased electricity output, and safeguarding and using our training data effectively. It also means promoting our global champions in critical components.

If not in this action plan, where will we see such a pledge from the Commission?

2-0297-0000.sourceText:
Senhor Presidente, Senhora Comissária Virkkunen, a discussão sobre a cibersegurança e a inteligência artificial não é apenas uma discussão sobre a capacidade de resistir a ataques cibernéticos ou de prevenir usos prejudiciais da tecnologia.

É também, e sobretudo, uma discussão sobre o direito dos povos ao seu desenvolvimento, sobre a cooperação internacional e a partilha de conhecimento científico, sobre a capacidade de garantir a coesão, esbatendo as assimetrias nacionais, e uma discussão também sobre a garantia dos direitos fundamentais dos cidadãos em geral, incluindo nos seus dados pessoais.

É absolutamente imprescindível que seja definida de forma clara a responsabilidade dos Estados em matéria de controlo e fiscalização do funcionamento de equipamentos e redes de comunicação. Deixar essas questões nas mãos das grandes multinacionais que operam nestas áreas não é solução.

É absolutamente essencial definir estratégias nacionais de desenvolvimento científico e tecnológico, robustecer estruturas públicas de investigação e desenvolvimento, qualificar recursos humanos. Também o desenvolvimento da infraestrutura tecnológica e de comunicações tem de ser orientado para estes objetivos.
2-0297-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Commissioner Virkkunen, the discussion on cybersecurity and artificial intelligence is not just a discussion about the ability to resist cyberattacks or prevent harmful uses of technology.

It is also, and above all, a discussion about the right of peoples to their development, about international cooperation and the sharing of scientific knowledge, about the ability to guarantee cohesion by blurring national asymmetries, and also a discussion about guaranteeing the fundamental rights of citizens in general, including regarding their personal data.

It is absolutely essential that the responsibility of States in terms of control and supervision of the operation of communication equipment and networks is clearly defined. Leaving these issues in the hands of the large multinationals operating in these areas is not a solution.

It is absolutely essential to define national strategies for scientific and technological development, to strengthen public research and development structures, and to train human resources. The development of technological and communications infrastructure must also be geared towards these objectives.

2-0298-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, dear colleagues, the Commission presented its action plan on cybersecurity and AI. It promises to make Europe a global leader in artificial intelligence. But leadership is not declared in a PR strategy; it is demonstrated when the technologies that matter are developed.

And recently, the American company Anthropic presented Mythos, an AI model capable of identifying complex chains of software vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed, and access was restricted to a small group of trusted partners to strengthen cyber defence. And guess what? The European Union was not among these trusted partners. That should concern every Member State, because cybersecurity is no longer just about writing standards, it is about who has access to cutting-edge AI. As the saying goes, America innovates and the EU regulates.

For years, Europe has focused on regulation and keeps being the master regulator. The AI Act is one of the world's most comprehensive regulatory frameworks, and yet today the most advanced cyber capabilities are emerging outside the EU. We regulate the technology while others build it. The EU supervises the market and others decide who gets access.

So I ask the Commission, how does this action plan make Europe a leader in AI and cybersecurity, and not just a regulator of technologies developed somewhere...?

(The President cut off the speaker)

2-0299-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, honourable Members, thank you very much for your interventions. As you very rightly highlighted here, two aspects are key today: how to now ensure access to these models and also how to build European sovereignty in this field.

So first, on access: we have already our AI Act in place and this blueprint, what we are now proposing, will not impose new mandatory or legal requirements for providers of AI models, but it will be a guidance document clarifying and providing more transparency around staged release and vetting processes, so how to have access and who should have access. It will allow us now to reinforce European leverage and make things easier for European players. And as we know that the question of access is now highly topical in international forums, we also think that this blueprint can really become a common global reference on access to frontier AI models.

Second, on Europe's sovereignty, here too, we are not starting from scratch, as we know. We have already made significant investments in developing our own AI compute infrastructure, in particular through the AI factories and also future gigafactories. But to build our own sovereign frontier AI capabilities, we need to mobilise massive additional private investments. And this is why the new strategic tech facility for Europe could be a game-changer here. But at the same time, everything we can really do to accelerate our savings and investments union, make more out of our single market, make it easier for our companies to scale up in Europe. Of course, all this will be crucial for our tech sovereignty.

And when we are looking at our resilience, of course, the coordination and response mechanism must also keep pace with the latest AI developments. And this is why now the revision of the Cybersecurity Act is so important, because it will now strengthen our ENISA and also equip the EU with the tools it needs to help secure our supply chains. And this is also why the proposal for a single entry point for cybersecurity incident reporting in the digital omnibus matters so much. I therefore count on both co-legislators to move these negotiations now forward swiftly and with the level of ambition that the security of our Union requires.

2-0300-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, Commissioner, artificial intelligence, without the slightest doubt, is becoming a core element of Europe's security architecture. The presentation of the action plan on cybersecurity and AI comes at a very decisive moment.

Today, we need a pragmatic approach. Europe must reduce strategic risks in its critical infrastructure. The revised Cybersecurity Act should give us proper, stronger tools to de‑risk mobile telecommunication networks from unsound third country suppliers, building on the lessons of the 5G security toolbox. Cybersecurity cannot depend on suppliers whose risk profile we cannot fully control.

Second, the dual nature of generative AI needs to be addressed. Large language models can be used to automate attacks or scale disinformation operation, and they can become targets themselves through model poisoning, data breaches or manipulation of training data.

Finally, we should not look at AI only as a threat. Properly governed AI can become a powerful instrument for defence, improving code review and strengthening incident response. The task before us is therefore very clear: Europe must regulate risk but also build capacity. We need a trusted infrastructure and secure AI system.

Cybersecurity and AI are now inseparable. Our response must be equally integrated.

2-0301-0000.sourceText:
Herr Präsident, Frau Kommissarin, verehrte Kolleginnen und Kollegen! Viele Kolleginnen und Kollegen haben von hier aus schon darauf hingewiesen, wie hoch die Sicherheitsrisiken mittlerweile im Cyber-Raum geworden sind. Und es ist ja eine alltägliche Erfahrung mittlerweile, dass entweder kriminelle Quellen oder Drittstaaten, die es mit der Sicherheit der Europäischen Union nicht so richtig gut meinen, uns immer wieder an der Stelle angreifen. Es ist keine abstrakte Gefahr – sie ist komplex und konkret, und sie ist alltäglich.

Machen wir es mal an einem Beispiel deutlich: deutsche Offshore-Windkraftanlagen – in denen sind Sensoren verbaut aus einem Land außerhalb der EU, und sie werden von dort überwacht. Das heißt also, wenn etwas mit dieser Windkraftanlage nicht in Ordnung ist, dann melden das diese Sensoren und sie führen dazu – so wenigstens der Plan –, dass sie repariert wird. Aber in diesen Drittstaaten gibt es einen death switch, d. h. man kann diese Anlagen ausschalten, wann immer man will. Und ich finde, einer der wichtigen Sicherheitsaspekte müsste sein, dass es in Zukunft keinen death switch mehr gibt und Daten auf Servern sind, die der EU-Gesetzgebung unterliegen.
2-0301-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Commissioner, dear colleagues!
Many colleagues have already pointed out from here how high security risks have now become in cyber space. And it is now an everyday experience that either criminal sources or third countries that do not mean particularly well with the security of the European Union attack us time and again at this point. It is not an abstract danger – it is complex and concrete, and it is everyday.
Let us make this clear with an example: German offshore wind turbines – in which sensors are installed from a country outside the EU, and they are monitored from there. That means, if something is not right with this wind turbine, then these sensors report it and they lead – at least according to the plan – to it being repaired. But in these third countries there is a death switch, i.e. you can switch off these facilities whenever you want. And I think one of the important security aspects should be that in future there is no longer a death switch and data is on servers that are subject to EU legislation.

2-0302-0000.sourceText:
Monsieur le Président, Madame la Vice-Présidente, chers collègues, alors aujourd’hui vous nous présentez le nouveau plan d’action de la Commission européenne sur la cybersécurité et l’intelligence artificielle. Les États-Unis ont Mythos, la Chine à DeepSeek, et l’Union européenne a un plan d’action. Plutôt, je dirais, un plan en réaction – encore une fois. En réaction à l’interdiction imposée par l’administration américaine d’accéder à Mythos, d’Anthropic, aux non-Américains – interdiction depuis levée.

Ce plan repose sur des formules qui sonnent comme des incantations: créer une capacité européenne des modèles d’IA, donner un cadre européen pour l’accès structuré aux capacités d’IA en cybersécurité, une énième plateforme européenne sécurisée pour tester les modèles d’IA avancés, un grand défi européen pour faire émerger des solutions de cybersécurité fondées sur l’IA.

Mais voici le paradoxe: d’un côté, la Commission met des solutions européennes – OK, très bien, on est tous d’accord –, mais, de l’autre, elle signe le traité Pax Silica, rédigé par ce sous-secrétaire d’État américain qui assume son opposition à la souveraineté numérique. Résultat: vous venez d’obliger les Européens à acheter des puces américaines et 750 milliards de dollars de GNL. Or, sans maîtrise de l’architecture des microprocesseurs ou de notre indépendance énergétique, les Américains pourront toujours nous déconnecter quand bon leur semblera.

Pourtant, une solution existe: un vrai consortium européen avec ASML, cette entreprise néerlandaise de semi-conducteurs, ou les terres rares de Guyane, mais vous avez encore choisi la dépendance. Alors, à quoi bon nous parler d’indépendance, de souveraineté, quand, de l’autre main, vous signez encore notre soumission? Les plans, c’est bien, l’action c’est mieux!
2-0302-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Madam Vice-President, dear colleagues, today you are presenting the European Commission's new action plan on cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.
The United States has Mythos, China has DeepSeek, and the European Union has an action plan. Rather, I would say, a reactive plan - yet again.
In reaction to the ban imposed by the US administration on non-Americans accessing Anthropic's Mythos - a ban since lifted.
This plan relies on formulas that sound like incantations: creating a European AI model capability, providing a European framework for structured access to AI capabilities in cybersecurity, yet another secure European platform for testing advanced AI models, a major European challenge to bring out AI-based cybersecurity solutions.
But here is the paradox: on the one hand, the Commission puts forward European solutions - OK, very good, we all agree - but, on the other hand, it signs the Pax Silica treaty, drafted by that US Under-Secretary of State who assumes his opposition to digital sovereignty.
Result: you have just forced Europeans to buy American chips and 750 billion dollars of LNG.
However, without control over microprocessor architecture or our energy independence, the Americans will always be able to disconnect us whenever they see fit.
Yet a solution exists: a real European consortium with ASML, that Dutch semiconductor company, or the rare earths of French Guiana, but you have chosen dependence once again.
So what is the point of talking to us about independence and sovereignty when, with the other hand, you are still signing our submission?
Plans are good, action is better!

2-0303-0000.sourceText:
Señor presidente, señora comisaria, la inteligencia artificial ya está teniendo impacto en todos nosotros, en nuestras relaciones personales, en nuestro negocio y en nuestra vida diaria. En todo.

Antes encontrábamos datos, comparábamos información, formábamos nuestra propia opinión. Hoy preguntamos a la IA y lo damos todo por válido, y eso puede convertirse en un gran problema, en un problema muy serio.

Si esa inteligencia artificial es atacada, manipulada o alterada de forma maliciosa, no solo estarán en riesgo nuestros datos, también estarán en riesgo nuestras opiniones, nuestras decisiones y nuestras libertades. En definitiva, estará en riesgo nuestra percepción.

Y en ciberseguridad ocurre algo parecido. Antes hablábamos de hackers intentando acceder a nuestros sistemas durante ciertas horas. Ahora tenemos bots que están intentando atacar nuestros sistemas veinticuatro horas al día, siete días a la semana, intentando aprender, adaptándose y buscando acceder a los datos más sensibles.

Por eso, Europa debe actuar, pero no puede hacerlo solo desde la regulación. Debemos facilitar la creación y —más importante— la permanencia de empresas en Europa. Debemos trabajar con la industria tecnológica, con los desarrolladores de software, con los grandes proveedores de nube, con las empresas de ciberseguridad y con quienes lideran la inteligencia artificial. Solo así estaremos por delante de quienes quieren buscar debilitar nuestras empresas, manipular a nuestros ciudadanos y socavar nuestras libertades. Protejamos Europa, pero hagámoslo...

(el presidente retira la palabra al orador)
2-0303-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Madam Commissioner, artificial intelligence is already having an impact on all of us, in our personal relationships, in our business and in our daily lives. On everything.

Before, we used to find data, compare information, and form our own opinions. Today we ask AI and take everything as valid, and that can become a big problem, a very serious problem.

If that artificial intelligence is maliciously attacked, manipulated or altered, not only will our data be at risk, but our opinions, our decisions and our freedoms will also be at risk. Ultimately, our perception will be at risk.

And something similar happens in cybersecurity. Before, we used to talk about hackers trying to access our systems during certain hours. Now we have bots trying to attack our systems twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, trying to learn, adapting and seeking to access the most sensitive data.

That is why Europe must act, but it cannot do so solely through regulation. We must facilitate the creation and—more importantly—the permanence of companies in Europe. We must work with the tech industry, with software developers, with major cloud providers, with cybersecurity companies and with those who lead artificial intelligence. Only in this way will we be ahead of those who want to weaken our companies, manipulate our citizens and undermine our freedoms. Let us protect Europe, but let us do so...

(the President cuts off the speaker)

2-0304-0000.sourceText:
Monsieur le Président, chers collègues, ayons confiance! Ayons confiance en nos entreprises européennes d’intelligence artificielle et investissons dès maintenant les milliards d’euros nécessaires au développement de nos propres modèles d’intelligence artificielle avancée!

La décision du président Trump de restreindre l’accès aux modèles américains d’IA les plus performants ne fait que confirmer ce que nous, libéraux et démocrates, dénoncions depuis son arrivée au pouvoir: un pays qui se sert de notre dépendance contre nous n’est pas un allié fiable. L’indépendance numérique doit être notre priorité, car c’est elle qui déterminera l’avenir de l’Europe.

Je salue les annonces que vous avez faites, Madame la Commissaire, pour notre cybersécurité face aux dangers nouveaux que représente l’IA, et nous vous soutiendrons pour toute mesure nouvelle que vous prendrez pour renforcer notre indépendance européenne dans l’intelligence artificielle et la cybersécurité.
2-0304-0000.englishText:
Mr President, dear colleagues, let us have confidence! Let us have confidence in our European artificial intelligence companies and invest right now the billions of euros necessary for the development of our own advanced artificial intelligence models!

President Trump's decision to restrict access to the highest-performing American AI models merely confirms what we, liberals and democrats, have been denouncing since he came to power: a country that uses our dependence against us is not a reliable ally. Digital independence must be our priority, because it is what will determine Europe's future.

I welcome the announcements you have made, Madam Commissioner, regarding our cybersecurity in the face of the new dangers represented by AI, and we will support you in any new measure you take to strengthen our European independence in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity.

2-0305-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, the industrial revolution was a miracle. We now live longer, work less and live better today than kings did 300 years ago. But before we got here, we had child labour, colonial exploitation and a climate catastrophe we are still living through.

The next industrial revolution is already happening. AI could unlock energy efficiency gains, design new cures for diseases, help fight world hunger or accelerate scientific discoveries. But what will we have to go through this time? Overheat our burning planet with ever-bigger data centres? Destroy jobs faster than we can adapt, or unleash a new era of cybercrime?

There are risks and opportunities. This action plan on AI and cybersecurity is a good first step, but I urge national leaders to put it higher on the agenda, organise a European Council summit dedicated to AI and unite around a plan to minimise risks and seize opportunities the European way.

2-0306-0000.sourceText:
�� Señor presidente, señorías, durante el minuto que dura mi intervención, el patrimonio de Elon Musk habrá aumentado 280 000 dólares, el de Zuckerberg 74 000 dólares, el de Bezos habrá aumentado 40 000 dólares. Insisto, solamente en un minuto.

Y mientras los oligarcas amigos de Trump se enriquecen, ¿para qué nos sirve la IA? ¿Para vivir mejor, para que los avances científicos se pongan al servicio del interés general? Pues no.

Mire, señora comisaria, hoy en la cumbre de la OTAN todos ustedes le prometerán a Donald Trump más aumento del gasto militar, más guerra y, sobre todo, también comprar precisamente servicios y sistemas de inteligencia artificial para sus amigos, los amigos de Donald Trump. Justo, por cierto, la misma semana que Donald Trump ha reconocido que sus hijos —que se dedican a fabricar drones militares— han tenido acceso a información privilegiada sobre las decisiones de Donald Trump. Supongo que también habrá tenido acceso a la información sobre cómo Trump impone a esta Europa sumisa las decisiones, a esta Europa sumisa respecto al imperialismo estadounidense.

Eso es todo lo que ustedes les ofrecen a los europeos, por parte de la Comisión Europea: guerra, más aumento del gasto militar, sumisión y mucho poder para los...

(el presidente retira la palabra a la oradora)

(La oradora se niega a que Diego Solier le formule una pregunta con arreglo al procedimiento de la «tarjeta azul»)
2-0306-0000.englishText:
Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, during the minute that my speech lasts, Elon Musk's wealth will have increased by $280,000, Zuckerberg's by $74,000, and Bezos's will have increased by $40,000. I insist, in just one minute.

And while Trump's oligarch friends get richer, what is AI used for? To live better, to put scientific advances at the service of the general interest? Well, no.

Look, Madam Commissioner, today at the NATO summit all of you will promise Donald Trump further increases in military spending, more war and, above all, also precisely to buy artificial intelligence services and systems for your friends, Donald Trump's friends. Right, by the way, the same week that Donald Trump has acknowledged that his children —who are engaged in manufacturing military drones— have had access to privileged information about Donald Trump's decisions. I suppose they will also have had access to information on how Trump imposes decisions on this submissive Europe, on this submissive Europe regarding US imperialism.

That is all you offer Europeans, on the part of the European Commission: war, a further increase in military spending, submission and a lot of power for the...

(the President cuts off the speaker)

(The speaker refuses to allow Diego Solier to ask a question under the 'blue card' procedure)
2-0306-0000.factCheck: Although Donald Trump's sons have invested in drone companies, Trump did not acknowledge that they had access to privileged information; rather, during a July 2026 CNBC interview, he argued that because presidential policies affect the entire economy, any business decision his children make could be perceived as involving 'inside information.'

2-0307-0000.sourceText:
�� Panie Przewodniczący! Ta debata jest o rzeczy oczywistej. Sztuczna inteligencja może współtworzyć obronność europejską, ale może też atakować nasze systemy i wtedy jest bardzo groźna, czyli może przynosić korzyści, ale wiąże się też z ryzykiem. No i pytanie: czy naszą odpowiedzią będzie realna odporność Europy, czy kolejny segregator procedur, których już mamy wystarczająco dużo?

My dzisiaj przegrywamy wyścig technologiczny przez to, że boimy się ryzyka, mamy nadmiar regulacji, i odnoszę wrażenie, że nadal wierzymy, że innowacje da się zadekretować w Brukseli. A tak nie jest, bo rozwój nie dzieje się dzięki regulacjom. Rozwój dzieje się dzięki temu, że ludzie mają swobodę działania, i jeżeli ten nowy plan będzie oznaczał tylko nowe obowiązki, audyty i certyfikaty, na które będzie stać tylko i wyłącznie gigantów, na które będzie stać tylko wielkie korporacje, to małe europejskie firmy AI nie będą w stanie zbudować nam i zabezpieczyć nam cyberbezpieczeństwa. One po prostu wyjadą albo zostaną klientami Amerykanów i Chińczyków. A wierzę, że może być inaczej.

(Mówca nie zgodził się na pytanie zasygnalizowane przez podniesienie niebieskiej kartki przez Nicolae Ștefănuță)
2-0307-0000.englishText:
Mr President! This debate is about something obvious. Artificial intelligence can co-create European defence, but it can also attack our systems and then it is very dangerous, meaning it can bring benefits, but it is also associated with risks. And the question is: will our response be real European resilience, or another binder of procedures, of which we already have enough?

Today we are losing the technological race because we are afraid of risk, we have an excess of regulation, and I have the impression that we still believe that innovation can be decreed in Brussels. And that is not the case, because development does not happen thanks to regulation. Development happens because people have the freedom to act, and if this new plan means only new obligations, audits and certificates that only and exclusively giants can afford, that only large corporations can afford, small European AI companies will not be able to build and secure our cybersecurity. They will simply leave or become clients of the Americans and the Chinese. And I believe that it can be different.

(The speaker agreed to take a question indicated by Nicolae Ștefănuță raising a blue card)

2-0308-0000.sourceText:
Monsieur le Président, chers collègues, Madame la Vice-Présidente, deux ans après le rapport Draghi, moins d’un tiers de ses recommandations ont été suivies.

Si nos infrastructures sont essentielles, l’Europe ne peut ignorer deux autres leviers stratégiques: les talents et le financement.

Nous formons d’excellents ingénieurs en cyber et en IA, mais les laissons partir peupler la Silicon Valley, affaiblissant ainsi notre capacité d’innovation. Il est temps de construire le récit d’une Europe fière de ses talents, capable de les valoriser pour les retenir. Cela passe aussi par une meilleure rémunération.

Nous devons également alléger la réglementation trop complexe qui mobilise une part excessive des budgets de mise en conformité. Quatre start-ups sur dix envisagent de quitter l’Union européenne pour cette raison.

Enfin, l’Europe doit changer d’échelle en matière de financement. Lorsque Arthur Mensch, fondateur de Mistral, lève 3 milliards, son plus petit concurrent américain, lui, lève 30 milliards.

Il est temps, chers collègues, de bâtir un véritable Nasdaq européen. Le sursaut ne peut plus attendre.
2-0308-0000.englishText:
Mr President, dear colleagues, Madam Vice-President, two years after the Draghi report, less than a third of its recommendations have been followed.

While our infrastructure is essential, Europe cannot ignore two other strategic levers: talent and financing.

We train excellent cyber and AI engineers, but let them leave to populate Silicon Valley, thereby weakening our innovation capacity. It is time to build the narrative of a Europe proud of its talent, capable of valuing them to retain them. This also involves better pay.

We must also ease overly complex regulation that ties up an excessive share of compliance budgets. Four out of ten start-ups are considering leaving the European Union for this reason.

Finally, Europe must scale up in terms of financing. When Arthur Mensch, founder of Mistral, raises 3 billion, his smallest American competitor raises 30 billion.

It is time, dear colleagues, to build a true European Nasdaq. The awakening can wait no longer.

2-0309-0000.sourceText:
Senhor Presidente, Senhora Comissária, Colegas, imagine-se um hospital onde um médico se prepara para assistir um doente. De repente, os sistemas informáticos deixam de responder. Não, não se trata de uma falha técnica. Foi, sim, um ciberataque.

Hoje, com recurso à inteligência artificial, esse ataque pode ser preparado, adaptado e lançado em poucos minutos, mas a mesma tecnologia pode também detetar a ameaça, conter a sua propagação, impedir que os serviços essenciais sejam interrompidos.

É esta a nova realidade da cibersegurança. A inteligência artificial já não é apenas uma ferramenta de inovação, é também uma ferramenta de defesa e, infelizmente, uma ferramenta ao serviço de quem procura explorar as nossas vulnerabilidades.

A Europa tem todas as condições para liderar esta transformação, mas só o conseguirá se souber equilibrar inovação, segurança e competitividade. É precisamente por isso que o plano de ação hoje apresentado é tão importante. Precisamos de investir num verdadeiro ecossistema europeu de cibersegurança, capaz de reunir conhecimento, talento, inovação e cooperação entre os Estados-Membros.

Precisamos de apoiar as pequenas e médias empresas, reforçar a partilha de informação sobre ameaças e garantir que a segurança acompanhe o desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial, desde a conceção das tecnologias.

Quando falamos de cibersegurança, não estamos apenas a proteger computadores ou redes. Estamos a proteger hospitais, escolas, empresas, serviços públicos essenciais e, acima de tudo, as nossas pessoas.

(O orador aceita responder a uma pergunta «cartão azul»)
2-0309-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Madam Commissioner, colleagues, imagine a hospital where a doctor is getting ready to treat a patient. Suddenly, the IT systems stop responding. No, it is not a technical failure. It was, in fact, a cyberattack.

Today, using artificial intelligence, such an attack can be prepared, adapted and launched in a few minutes, but the same technology can also detect the threat, contain its spread, and prevent essential services from being interrupted.

This is the new reality of cybersecurity. Artificial intelligence is no longer just a tool for innovation, it is also a tool for defence and, unfortunately, a tool at the service of those who seek to exploit our vulnerabilities.

Europe has all the conditions to lead this transformation, but it will only succeed if it knows how to balance innovation, security and competitiveness. This is precisely why the action plan presented today is so important. We need to invest in a true European cybersecurity ecosystem, capable of bringing together knowledge, talent, innovation and cooperation among Member States.

We need to support small and medium-sized enterprises, strengthen the sharing of information on threats, and ensure that security keeps pace with the development of artificial intelligence, right from the design of technologies.

When we talk about cybersecurity, we are not just protecting computers or networks. We are protecting hospitals, schools, businesses, essential public services and, above all, our people.

(The speaker agrees to take a "blue card" question)

2-0310-0000.sourceText:
Senhor Presidente, Senhor Deputado Paulo Cunha, imagine milhares de alunos à espera dos resultados dos exames nacionais por uma falha informática dos serviços do Ministério da Educação em Portugal. Não precisa de imaginar, está a acontecer.

A minha pergunta é: não vale a pena falarmos sobre grandes discursos sobre a inovação, é preciso ter responsabilidade e que a administração pública respeite os cidadãos, responda com clareza e, por isso, pergunto-lhe de quem é a responsabilidade do que está a acontecer em Portugal, que está a deixar milhares de alunos com o futuro comprometido pelos erros informáticos da administração pública na correção dos seus exames?
2-0310-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Mr Paulo Cunha, imagine thousands of students waiting for national exam results due to an IT failure by the Ministry of Education services in Portugal. You do not need to imagine it, it is happening.

My question is: it is not worth having grand speeches about innovation, what is needed is responsibility and for the public administration to respect citizens, respond with clarity and, therefore, I ask you whose responsibility is what is happening in Portugal, which is leaving thousands of students with their futures compromised by the IT errors of the public administration in grading their exams?

2-0311-0000.sourceText:
(início da intervenção com o microfone desligado)... informada porque não está a acontecer nada do que disse, muito menos pelas causas que invocou.

As circunstâncias são diferentes, senhora deputada. O que está em causa é uma mudança, uma evolução.

A senhora deputada prefere o imobilismo, o passadismo, a manutenção, a perseverança no erro e a recusa da inovação e da mudança.

Está em causa uma mudança e as consequências para os alunos e para as comunidades não são tão graves como aquelas que aponta.
2-0311-0000.englishText:
(start of the intervention with the microphone off)... informed because nothing of what you said is happening, much less for the causes you invoked.

The circumstances are different, Madam Member. What is at stake is a change, an evolution.

You prefer standstill, backwardness, maintenance, perseverance in error, and the refusal of innovation and change.

What is at stake is change, and the consequences for students and communities are not as serious as those you point out.

2-0312-0000.sourceText:
Senhor Presidente, Senhora Comissária, nós tivemos oportunidade, recentemente, de falar na Comissão. Queria saudar o plano de ação, apesar de ter chegado apenas no início deste debate. Quero saudar a apresentação, porque é mais um instrumento que ajuda a que todos percebamos como os Estados-Membros devem responder com a inteligência artificial e com mais cibersegurança.

E não, eu não trouxe aqui, a este plenário, um caso utópico. Ele está a acontecer em Portugal e nós estamos a falar de sistemas críticos. E quando uma falha informática, pela implementação da transição digital, põe em causa o futuro de milhares de jovens, estamos a falar de uma transição digital que não está a cuidar da igualdade de oportunidades para todos.

E o meu apelo, Senhora Comissária, é que com este plano de ação, onde exorta os Estados-Membros a que tenham mais coordenação, eu exorto a que haja mais coordenação, maior responsabilidade e melhor capacidade de colocar a inteligência artificial ao serviço das nossas democracias, ao serviço da igualdade de oportunidades, ao serviço dos nossos cidadãos.
2-0312-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Madam Commissioner, we recently had the opportunity to speak in the Committee. I would like to welcome the action plan, even though it only arrived at the beginning of this debate. I want to welcome the presentation because it is yet another instrument that helps us all understand how Member States should respond with artificial intelligence and more cybersecurity.

And no, I did not bring a utopian case here to this plenary. It is happening in Portugal and we are talking about critical systems. And when an IT failure, due to the implementation of the digital transition, jeopardises the future of thousands of young people, we are talking about a digital transition that is not taking care of equal opportunities for everyone.

And my appeal, Madam Commissioner, is that with this action plan, where you urge Member States to have more coordination, I urge that there be more coordination, greater responsibility and a better capacity to put artificial intelligence at the service of our democracies, at the service of equal opportunities, at the service of our citizens.

2-0313-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, the European Commission's response to the rise of AI and related cybersecurity challenges is disappointing, to say the least, including the new action plan.

When the US learned that Germany was building a nuclear weapon, it understood that it must do the same. In fact, it understood that it must win the race. When the first atomic bomb was built, others were rushing to catch up. Those who belonged to the nuclear club set the rules.

Today, the same applies to AI. Europe cannot set the rules if it has no serious sovereign AI capability. You talk about a massive private investment in order to boost frontier sovereign AI capability. But you are late.

And you cannot fix this by focusing on AI alone. We need to increase the training of software engineers, incentivise automation in industry, develop and build chips, guarantee cheap energy. Otherwise, private investors won't invest in AI in Europe. Public procurement is therefore absolutely necessary.

We talk about European digital sovereignty again and again in this House, and then nothing meaningful happens. The European Commission published yet another action plan that is news today and will be forgotten tomorrow. Why? Because the US and China, who really are serious about the AI race, will publish a new model and we'll be starting this debate all over again.

We need to set benchmarks, deadlines on how the EU will catch up on AI.

(The speaker agreed to take a blue-card question)

2-0314-0000.sourceText:
So I will ask you something because you mentioned software engineers. Did you know that right now, the biggest victim in the industry of including more AI, it's exactly software engineers? Did you know that companies do not hire people fresh off the benches of universities anymore because they use more AI to cut costs?

Do you think or not, that we have a social problem, or that we might have an even bigger social problem, because lots of ICT graduates are not entering the market because everything is used with AI? And what do we do with the massive unemployment generated by that? Do you also see a danger...?

(The President cut off the speaker)

2-0315-0000.sourceText:
You've raised several issues which deal with generally how we're going to apply AI. Of course it touches on software engineers as well. That's why I argued in favour of public procurement, because private investment is not happening in AI or not sufficiently in Europe. That's why we should have massive public procurement. To suck up also the engineers, we should incentivise software engineers and then provide them with the job of doing so.

In a certain way, we should be treating AI and the development of AI, just like I said in my example, like a nuclear weapon, like a matter of national security and of strategic importance. And when we talk about a sector of strategic importance and defence, like in cybersecurity, we need to have a public procurement push.

2-0316-0000.sourceText:
Signor Presidente, onorevoli colleghi, nel dibattito che in questi mesi si sta svolgendo sul ruolo che l'Europa dovrebbe andare a ricoprire nel campo dello sviluppo dell'intelligenza artificiale, tra chi vorrebbe un'Europa all'inseguimento di Stati Uniti e Cina e chi invece sogna un'Europa capace di valorizzare le proprie eccellenze grazie all'intelligenza artificiale, Commissaria, non sottovalutiamo il tema della sicurezza e della cibersicurezza.

Perché, se vogliamo proteggere i nostri dati, se vogliamo proteggere le nostre infrastrutture, se vogliamo proteggere le nostre aziende, l'intelligenza artificiale è e può essere un alleato fondamentale.

Nel campo della cibersicurezza – Lei lo sa molto meglio di me – l'Europa oggi non deve inseguire, non è arretrata: l'Europa oggi è leader in questo settore. Allora, grazie all'intelligenza artificiale, possiamo porci un obiettivo: diventare lo spazio digitale più sicuro al mondo.
2-0316-0000.englishText:
Mr President, honourable colleagues, in the debate that has been taking place in recent months on the role that Europe should play in the field of artificial intelligence development, between those who would like a Europe chasing the United States and China and those who instead dream of a Europe capable of enhancing its own areas of excellence thanks to artificial intelligence, Commissioner, let us not underestimate the issue of security and cybersecurity.

Because if we want to protect our data, if we want to protect our infrastructure, if we want to protect our companies, artificial intelligence is and can be a fundamental ally.

In the field of cybersecurity – you know this much better than I do – Europe today does not need to catch up, it is not lagging behind: Europe today is a leader in this sector. So, thanks to artificial intelligence, we can set ourselves a goal: to become the most secure digital space in the world.

2-0317-0000.sourceText:
Hr. formand! Kunstig intelligens har ændret cybersikkerhed fundamentalt. Det giver os et stærkere forsvar, men det giver også vores angribere stærkere våben. Derfor har Europa brug for handling, og vi har brug for handling nu!

Den vigtigste opgave er ikke nødvendigvis – som nogen af kollegerne peger på – flere regler. Den vigtigste opgave er at sikre, at europæiske virksomheder og myndigheder faktisk har adgang til de bedste værktøjer, og med kommissærens handlingsplan har vi faktisk taget et skridt i den rigtige retning. Så tak for det!

Det er en vigtig pointe, at vi ikke skal ty til de sædvanlige europæiske løsninger her, nemlig flere regler. Cybersikkerhed er ikke kun et spørgsmål om sikkerhed, det er også blevet et spørgsmål om konkurrenceevne. Vi skal derfor have styrket den europæiske konkurrenceevne. Vi skal ikke regulere mere, vi skal investere mere i europæisk sikkerhed, europæisk AI, og det skal ske nu!
2-0317-0000.englishText:
Mr President! Artificial intelligence has fundamentally changed cybersecurity. It gives us a stronger defense, but it also gives our attackers stronger weapons. Therefore, Europe needs action, and we need action now!

The most important task is not necessarily – as some of our colleagues point out – more rules. The most important task is to ensure that European companies and authorities actually have access to the best tools, and with the Commissioner's action plan, we have actually taken a step in the right direction. So thank you for that!

It is an important point that we should not resort to the usual European solutions here, namely more rules. Cybersecurity is not only a matter of security, it has also become a matter of competitiveness. We must therefore strengthen European competitiveness. We must not regulate more, we must invest more in European security, European AI, and this must happen now!

2-0318-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, Madam Vice‑President, thank you so much for this action plan. And yet, OpenAI and Anthropic raise USD 122 billion and USD 30 billion, Mistral raises EUR 3 billion. OpenAI offers the American Government a 5 % stake, in Europe, we have no clear timeline for gigafactories. Washington cuts off access to Fable and Mythos, and the Commission to this day has no access to these models.

This town and this House are obsessed about deregulation. Regulation is not the problem. It is about equity. It is about funding. We have now the AI omnibus. Did it change anything on the ground? No. This Commission should convene a meeting between businesses, the big businesses of Europe, and demand that they put on the table trillions of euros in order to invest into our future. Because if they don't, we will not have future at all.

(The speaker agreed to take several blue-card questions)

2-0319-0000.sourceText:
Thank you, Mr Lagodinsky. You say that regulations in Europe are not a problem for the development of frontier AI models. I beg to differ. The copyright directive is very different from the US and China.

But let me just zoom in on one aspect of the GDPR. I'd like to have your opinion on it as an expert. If you make neural networks, you do a hypothesis – in the style of Sergey Lagodinsky, I want to set up a reasoning, which is hard because I'm not you, but AI can do that. In the GDPR, using your data is not allowed to train a model.

How are you willing to solve this? From the 3 000 AI large language models in the world, only 30 are European, 0 are compliant and we will have 0 new AI large language models if we do not deregulate.

2-0320-0000.sourceText: That is very interesting but we cannot have an academic debate. Please.

2-0321-0000.sourceText:
I would like to address one specific issue that you mentioned – the copyright directive. First of all, in the AI Act, we invested a lot in order to make it possible for training purposes to use our copyright. And we have a data mining exemption. We have an opportunity to use that and to use data for AI training.

So I don't think that this is the biggest challenge for frontier models to be based here. Nor do I think that GDPR, with all the exceptions that we have, has an opportunity to stop the development.

What we don't have and what we're lacking is equity and investment.

2-0322-0000.sourceText:
If I understand you well, you think the copyright directive or the GDPR are no hurdles to training large language models. But if we set up a hearing with AI experts, you and me together, very soon, on the shortest possible notice, and you find me one AI expert that confirms your lecture on this, we agree.

But I'm afraid I've spoken to dozens and they all disagree. It's impossible. So we have to deregulate, Mr Lagodinsky, and I'm hoping for your help.

2-0323-0000.sourceText:
It's not my first year and it's not my first month. I've been talking to experts. I've been talking to businesses for years, since I was one of the negotiators for the AI Act and the Data Act and many other things.

If you talk to people from Mistral, if you talk to people from Aleph Alpha, when Aleph Alpha was still alive, we were consulting with them and they're all saying this is not our biggest problem. The biggest problem is access to money. The biggest problem is compute, the infrastructure that we're trying to make here. That is something we should be focusing on instead of the tech whining that this House has been spending and wasting their time with.

2-0324-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, just to be real quick, am I also allowed to make a reference to the reply he gave to the first blue card? Or am I only allowed to make a reference to the original speech? Whatever I like. Lovely, OK.

Mr Lagodinsky, thank you very much for accepting the blue card. I listened to your speech and in the crescendo of your speech, you were talking very much on how important all of this is. And then in the fortissimo, you talked about the fact that we should sit down with businesses and demand that they invest money. How to force them? What do we do?

2-0325-0000.sourceText:
I'm sure they will not say no because they realise better than us that their future, both in terms of cybersecurity but also of security and also access to the frontier models, will be in our own capabilities. This is precisely what the Executive Vice‑President has said.

Our cybersecurity is our sovereignty, and our sovereignty is our capabilities. These companies, from Siemens to whatever the French counterparts are, depend on our ability to innovate here. And this ability depends on compute. And compute depends on equity – their equity. And it is in their interest for us to survive economically and in terms of innovation.

2-0326-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, it is true that we are facing a security crisis. Over the past year alone, we have seen an unprecedented number of software vulnerabilities discovered and exploited by malicious compliance actors.

Too often, policymakers repeat the dramatic claims made by large AI companies, without subjecting them to independent scrutiny. We should keep in mind that these companies have commercial interests. That is why the European Union must base its cybersecurity policy on independent evidence, rigorous analysis and our own strategic interest – not on narratives promoted by those who stand to benefit from them.

As we are discussing cybersecurity, I will seize the opportunity to present the case of Stelios Koulouglou, a former MEP from the last term who was spied on by Pegasus when he was a member of the committee investigating Pegasus in this House in the past term, as I said. If we let this abuse take place with no consequences, the message will be that any means can be deployed against the democratic mandate of this Parliament, and that is completely unacceptable.

2-0327-0000.sourceText:
Señor presidente, señora Virkkunen, con todos los respetos, pero, de verdad: cómo nos presenta hoy aquí un plan de ciberseguridad cuando han sido jaqueados dos veces en tres meses.

En marzo les robaron 350 GB de datos de sus propios funcionarios. Y, cuando hemos preguntado, nos hemos dado cuenta de dónde guardaban toda la soberanía tecnológica europea —a ver si lo adivina la Cámara—: en Amazon, en un servidor de Seattle. Esa es la soberanía tecnológica europea.

En fin, qué ridículo es esto. El 70 % de toda la nube europea pertenece a tres empresas americanas. Eso sí, nos felicitamos por lo modernos que somos porque aquí habéis prohibido que se utilice el wifi de los diputados para usar TikTok. Es alucinante.

¿No se da usted de que son como esa típica alumna que no estudia pero va con complejo de profesora y corrige absolutamente a todos los demás sobre qué tenemos que hacer bien o mal? 100 leyes digitales, 270 reguladores, Informe Draghi. Y mientras China está fabricando chips y Estados Unidos gigantes tecnológicos, ¿qué estamos haciendo nosotros? Formularios, certificados y más... (el presidente retira la palabra al orador).
2-0327-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Ms Virkkunen, with all due respect, but really: how can you present a cybersecurity plan here today when you have been hacked twice in three months.

In March, 350 GB of data belonging to your own officials was stolen from you. And when we asked, we realized where you were storing all European technological sovereignty — let's see if the House can guess it: on Amazon, on a server in Seattle. That is European technological sovereignty.

Anyway, how ridiculous this is. 70% of all the European cloud belongs to three American companies. Of course, we congratulate ourselves on how modern we are because here you have banned the use of the MPs' Wi-Fi to use TikTok. It is mind-blowing.

Do you not realize that you are like that typical student who does not study but has a teacher complex and corrects absolutely everyone else on what we have to do right or wrong? 100 digital laws, 270 regulators, the Draghi Report. And while China is manufacturing chips and the United States technological giants, what are we doing? Forms, certificates and more... (the President cuts off the speaker).

2-0328-0000.sourceText:
Herr Präsident, Frau Kommissarin! Künstliche Intelligenz wird zum entscheidenden Faktor für unsere Cybersecurity und damit auch für Europas Wettbewerbsfähigkeit, für Europas Souveränität und Resilienz. Wichtig, dass die Kommission nun einen Aktionsplan vorgelegt hat, denn eines ist klar: Europa darf bei den sogenannten Frontier‑KI‑Modellen nicht dauerhaft von Entscheidungen in anderen Drittstaaten abhängig sein.

Wenn der Zugang zu kritischen KI‑Modellen von heute auf morgen eingeschränkt werden kann, dann ist das nicht nur ein technologisches Problem, es ist vor allem ein Sicherheitsproblem für Europa. Daher habe ich auch einige Fragen an Sie: Ist eine europäische Evaluierungsstelle ab 2027 nicht zu spät? Technologische Entwicklung wartet nicht auf unsere EU‑Zeitpläne. Und wie stellen wir sicher, dass Europa bereits jetzt über die notwendigen Fähigkeiten verfügt, Risiken zu bewerten und gleichzeitig Innovationen zu ermöglichen?

Zweitens: Der Entwurf reagiert auf die Abhängigkeit von außereuropäischen KI-Modellen. Reicht ein europäischer Blueprint aus, oder braucht Europa nicht vor allem eigene leistungsfähige KI‑Modelle und Rechenkapazitäten? Und gerade die KMU liegen mir sehr am Herzen, sie verfügen aber nicht über große Rechenzentren oder über große Budgets. Wie werden wir sicherstellen, dass auch KMU einfachen Zugang zu vertrauenswürdigen europäischen KI‑Sicherheitslösungen erhalten?

Für mich ist klar: Digitale Souveränität entsteht nicht nur durch Ankündigung, sondern vor allem durch Geschwindigkeit und Wettbewerbsfähigkeit.
2-0328-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Commissioner! Artificial intelligence is becoming a decisive factor for our cybersecurity and thus also for Europe's competitiveness, Europe's sovereignty and resilience. It is important that the Commission has now presented an action plan, because one thing is clear: Europe must not remain permanently dependent on decisions in other third countries when it comes to so-called frontier AI models.

If access to critical AI models can be restricted overnight, that is not just a technological problem, it is above all a security problem for Europe. Therefore, I also have a few questions for you: Is a European evaluation body starting in 2027 not too late? Technological development does not wait for our EU timetables. And how do we ensure that Europe already has the necessary capabilities to assess risks while enabling innovation?

Secondly: The draft responds to the dependency on non-European AI models. Is a European blueprint enough, or does Europe not need, above all, its own powerful AI models and computing capacities? And SMEs are particularly close to my heart, but they do not have large data centres or large budgets. How will we ensure that SMEs too get easy access to trustworthy European AI security solutions?

For me it is clear: Digital sovereignty is created not only through announcements, but above all through speed and competitiveness.

2-0329-0000.sourceText:
Señor presidente, Europa ya ha demostrado que sabe regular la tecnología. Ahora tiene que demostrar que también sabe construirla.

Si en el siglo XX la soberanía se defendía con tanques y cañones, en el siglo XXI también se defiende con algoritmos, semiconductores o datos. Hace apenas unos días, la empresa estadounidense Palantir, proveedora de tecnologías de inteligencia y defensa, afirmaba que politizar la tecnología es un error, pero decidir quién desarrolla la inteligencia artificial que protege nuestras infraestructuras críticas —hospitales, parlamentos, bancos— no es una cuestión técnica, es profundamente política y existencial. Pero, mientras todavía debatimos la soberanía tecnológica de Europa, muchos de nuestros Gobiernos financian con dinero público muchas tecnologías críticas desarrolladas fuera de la Unión Europea.

Nadie construiría una casa para darle las llaves a otro. Europa tampoco puede hacerlo con su seguridad digital. Por eso, damos la bienvenida al plan de acción sobre ciberseguridad e IA presentado por la Comisión, pero necesitamos muchos más recursos: gastar más, pero sobre todo gastar «europeo», apoyar empresas europeas y gigafactorías para construir nuestra soberanía digital.
2-0329-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Europe has already shown that it knows how to regulate technology. Now it has to show that it also knows how to build it.

If in the 20th century sovereignty was defended with tanks and cannons, in the 21st century it is also defended with algorithms, semiconductors or data. Just a few days ago, the US company Palantir, a provider of intelligence and defence technologies, stated that politicising technology is a mistake, but deciding who develops the artificial intelligence that protects our critical infrastructure — hospitals, parliaments, banks — is not a technical question, it is profoundly political and existential. But, while we are still debating Europe's technological sovereignty, many of our governments use public money to fund many critical technologies developed outside the European Union.

No one would build a house only to hand the keys to someone else. Nor can Europe do that with its digital security. That is why we welcome the action plan on cybersecurity and AI presented by the Commission, but we need many more resources: to spend more, but above all to spend "European", to support European companies and gigafactories to build our digital sovereignty.

2-0330-0000.sourceText:
Herr Präsident, geschätzte Kollegen! Wir haben ja erst letztes Mal in Straßburg hier über die Elektrifizierungsinitiative von der Kommission gesprochen, die ja auch ähnliche Ausmaße annimmt wie das, was wir jetzt sehen. Und wir sagen ganz klar Ja zum Schutz, aber Nein zu einer Brüsseler Bürokratie-Krake.

Die KI macht Cyberangriffe smarter und gefährlicher – das wissen wir. Doch dieser Aktionsplan der Kommission droht wieder einmal ein Monster an Formularen, Berichtspflichten und Gebühren zu werden. Das schützt keinen Server und hilft vor allem den kleinen Betrieben nicht; statt echter Hilfe gibt es einmal mehr Verwaltung und Zentralisierung.

Wir müssen wachsam sein: Cybersicherheit darf keine Hintertür für Massenüberwachung und Meinungskontrolle werden. Unser klarer Kurs in dieser Sache heißt Ja zu realer Sicherheit, Nein zu Papierkram und Machtkonzentration in Brüssel und zu Freiheitsabbau für die Bürger.
2-0330-0000.englishText:
Mr President, dear colleagues! The last time we were here in Strasbourg, we spoke about the Commission's electrification initiative, which is also taking on dimensions similar to what we are seeing now. And we say a very clear yes to protection, but no to a Brussels bureaucratic octopus.

AI is making cyberattacks smarter and more dangerous – we know that. Yet once again, this action plan by the Commission threatens to become a monster of forms, reporting obligations and fees. That protects no server and above all does not help small businesses; instead of real help, there is once again administration and centralization.

We must be vigilant: cybersecurity must not become a backdoor for mass surveillance and opinion control. Our clear course in this matter is yes to real security, no to paperwork and the concentration of power in Brussels, and no to the reduction of freedom for citizens.

2-0331-0000.sourceText:
Domnule președinte, stimați colegi, o dronă maritimă ucraineană a fost aproape să distrugă recent portul Constanța din România, iar noi nu am avut capacitatea tehnică de a o opri. Un model de inteligență artificială controlat de forțe rău-intenționate poate paraliza o întreagă economie. Acestea sunt vulnerabilități reale ale Uniunii Europene, nu lipsa de reglementare.

Securitatea cibernetică se construiește prin investiții, prin competențe și prin tehnologii proprii. Nu putem vorbi despre suveranitate digitală câtă vreme tehnologiile critice rămân controlate din afara Uniunii. Europa trebuie să-și dezvolte propriile capacități, iar România, cu unul dintre cele mai performante ecosisteme IT din Europa, poate și trebuie să contribuie. Singura condiție este ca fondurile europene să ajungă și în estul Uniunii.

Statele membre trebuie să rămână actorii principali în securitatea națională și, nu în ultimul rând, combaterea criminalității cibernetice nu poate deveni pretext pentru supravegherea generalizată a cetățenilor.
2-0331-0000.englishText:
Mr President, dear colleagues, a Ukrainian maritime drone recently came close to destroying the port of Constanța in Romania, and we lacked the technical capacity to stop it. An artificial intelligence model controlled by malicious forces can paralyze an entire economy. These are real vulnerabilities of the European Union, not a lack of regulation.

Cybersecurity is built through investments, skills, and proprietary technologies. We cannot speak of digital sovereignty as long as critical technologies remain controlled from outside the Union. Europe must develop its own capabilities, and Romania, with one of the most high-performing IT ecosystems in Europe, can and must contribute. The only condition is that European funds also reach the east of the Union.

Member states must remain the primary actors in national security and, last but not least, combating cybercrime cannot become a pretext for the generalized surveillance of citizens.

2-0332-0000.sourceText:
Herr Präsident, liebe Kollegen! Von Großbanken über Mittelstand bis zur kritischen Infrastruktur – Europas Sicherheit hängt davon ab, ob KI‑Technologie hier entsteht und skalieren kann. Deshalb muss der Cybersecurity und AI Action Plan vor allem eins: Bürokratie abbauen, Investitionen ermöglichen und neue Technologien schneller in die Anwendung bringen.

Wenn in den USA und China in rasantem Tempo neue KI‑Modelle entstehen, schreibt Europa nach wie vor vor allen Dingen Regeln. Aber Cyberangriffe und technologische Abhängigkeit bekämpft man eben nicht mit Berichtspflichten, sondern mit technologischem Vorsprung. Europa wird sicherer, wenn die besten Technologien von hier kommen. Dafür brauchen wir weniger Bürokratie, mehr Kapital, günstigere Energie und einen echten europäischen Binnenmarkt, damit unsere klügsten Köpfe einfach mal machen können. Denn digitale Souveränität wächst nicht aus Abschottung, und Cybersecurity entsteht nicht in Gesetzestexten, sondern durch Innovation.

Hören wir auf, die Welt regulieren zu wollen! Zeigen wir der Welt endlich wieder, dass Europa sie verändern kann!
2-0332-0000.englishText:
Mr President, dear colleagues! From major banks and small and medium-sized enterprises to critical infrastructure – Europe's security depends on whether AI technology is developed and can scale here. That is why the Cybersecurity and AI Action Plan must do one thing above all: cut red tape, enable investment, and bring new technologies into application faster.

While new AI models are emerging at a rapid pace in the US and China, Europe continues above all to write rules. But cyberattacks and technological dependence are not combated with reporting obligations, but rather with a technological lead. Europe becomes more secure when the best technologies come from here. For this we need less bureaucracy, more capital, cheaper energy, and a genuine European single market so that our brightest minds can simply get on with it. Because digital sovereignty does not grow out of isolation, and cybersecurity does not emerge in legislative texts, but through innovation.

Let us stop trying to regulate the world! Let us finally show the world once again that Europe can change it!

2-0333-0000.sourceText:
Herr Präsident, Frau Kommissarin, liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen! Eine Quizfrage: Wie viele Ressourcen benötigt eine Minute KI-generiertes Video? 200 Kilowattstunden. Das ist der Stromverbrauch einer Durchschnittsfamilie an zwei Tagen. Sieben Liter Wasser, sauberes Trinkwasser, das unseren Bürgerinnen und Bürgern und auch unserer Landwirtschaft nicht mehr zur Verfügung steht. Die Techkonzerne haben nicht nur extremen Hunger nach Daten, sondern auch extremen Durst nach Wasser.

Deshalb: Ja, die EU muss im Digitalsektor unabhängiger werden, aber es kann nicht sein, dass knappe Ressourcen für die Profite Weniger geopfert werden, wenn diese auch noch obendrein keine Arbeitsplätze schaffen, sondern eher welche vernichten. Kluge Menschen lernen aus ihren Fehlern; weise lernen aus den Fehlern anderer. Der wachsende Widerstand gegen Datenzentren in den USA wegen steigender Strompreise, wegen der Wasserfrage, wegen Luftverschmutzung – daraus müssen wir lernen.

Deshalb: Wir brauchen Datenzentren – ja, mit klaren Regeln –, effiziente Technologie, erneuerbare Energien, Abwärmenutzung, Transparenz, Beteiligung der Bevölkerung: Dann wird daraus was.
2-0333-0000.englishText:
Mr President, Commissioner, dear colleagues! A quiz question: How many resources does one minute of AI-generated video require? 200 kilowatt hours. That is the electricity consumption of an average family in two days. Seven litres of water, clean drinking water that is no longer available to our citizens and also to our agriculture. Tech corporations have not only an extreme hunger for data, but also an extreme thirst for water.

Therefore: Yes, the EU must become more independent in the digital sector, but it cannot be the case that scarce resources are sacrificed for the profits of a few, especially when these on top of that do not create jobs, but rather destroy them. Wise people learn from their mistakes; the wise learn from the mistakes of others. The growing resistance to data centres in the USA due to rising electricity prices, due to the water issue, due to air pollution - we must learn from that.

Therefore: We need data centres - yes, with clear rules -, efficient technology, renewable energies, waste heat utilisation, transparency, public participation: Then something will come of it.

2-0334-0000.sourceText:
Hr. formand! Jeg synes det er ærgerligt, at Kommissionen ikke fremlægger sine forslag i så god tid, at vi har mulighed for at læse dem, inden vi skal diskutere dem. Det synes jeg er særlig ærgerligt, fordi der også i det her forslag faktisk er positive ting omkring udviklingen af open source og en strategi for det.

Men hvis vi for alvor tager EU's cybersikkerhed alvorligt, hvorfor skulle vi så ikke starte med at lukke helt åbenlyse huller? Hvorfor skifter vi ikke hurtigt EU væk fra programmer som Outlook, Webex og Teams og fylder dem ud med europæisk forankrede open source-programmer, der sikrer vores data og digitale suverænitet? Og jeg må også sige, at vi hører også advarsler om, at retsakten om udvikling af cloudtjenester og kunstig intelligens risikerer at ende som en "continuous American dependancy act". Og vi er vel enige om, at fortsat afhængighed af USA på det her område er et alvorligt problem for vores cybersikkerhed.
2-0334-0000.englishText:
Mr President! I think it is regrettable that the Commission does not present its proposals in good time so that we have the opportunity to read them before we have to discuss them. I think this is particularly regrettable because there are also positive things in this proposal regarding the development of open source and a strategy for it.

But if we really take the EU's cybersecurity seriously, why shouldn't we start by closing completely obvious gaps? Why don't we quickly shift the EU away from programmes like Outlook, Webex and Teams and fill them with European-anchored open source programmes that secure our data and digital sovereignty? And I must also say that we also hear warnings that the Cyber Resilience Act and AI Act risk ending up as a "continuous American dependency act". And surely we agree that continued dependence on the USA in this area is a serious problem for our cybersecurity.

2-0335-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, Commissioner, dear colleagues, the action plan on cybersecurity and AI is a welcome step in supporting our Member States and companies to navigate the digital transition. But regulation alone will not solve our innovation deficit or mitigate the threats we face.

In 2024, the United States produced 40 notable AI models, China produced 15, while Europe produced only three. We are heavily dependent on foreign cloud and other digital technologies. To bridge this gap, we need aggressive public‑private investment in European computing capacity, critical digital infrastructure, cloud computing, data centres and advanced connectivity. We have built a robust regulatory foundation with the Digital Markets Act, Cyber Resilience Act, etc. Now, we must ensure these frameworks are enforced effectively, and our own tech gets adequate financing. We should become creators, not only regulators.

Cybersecurity and AI are our security issue too. Last year, Europe recorded thousands of major cyber incidents, largely traced back to actors in Russia and China. In my home country, Lithuania, we recorded nearly 4 000 incidents, averaging 10 attacks every single day. Advanced AI is now making these threats exponentially more dangerous.

So let me stress this: Europe's security and competitiveness are only as strong as the technology we control.

2-0336-0000.sourceText:
Mr President, Commissioner, we cannot protect our hospitals, energy grids, public administrations and elections with tools that can disappear because of a decision taken in Washington or somewhere else outside the EU. Of course, we should cooperate with the United States, with companies and with other partners, but cooperation should never mean dependency.

I hope the action plan could answer three concrete questions. First, what does guarantee that the case with the ENISA and Anthropic will not happen again? Second, what is the timeline for building real European AI capability for cybersecurity, including for EU and national authorities, municipalities and companies? And third, where is the money?

So, Member States speak every day about security, defence and geopolitical threats, but then want to limit the EU budget when Europe needs the capacity to act. That is undermining our security while pretending to be sovereign. Digital sovereignty means public investment, democratic control and accountability, not simply subsidising a few private companies to build data centres in Europe.

We need an action plan with deadlines, funding and enforcement, not another strategy that sounds strong in Brussels, but leaving Europe vulnerable when the next surprises come.

2-0337-0000.sourceText:
Monsieur le Président, chers collègues, chaque apport à l’innovation technologique, chaque progrès humain s’est toujours accompagné de son lot de risques et de nouvelles vulnérabilités. L’intelligence artificielle n’y fera pas exception.

Motivés par des siècles d’expérience en matière de risques technologiques, nous serons avisés de nous assurer que l’IA ne devienne pas une nouvelle source de dépendance de nos nations. L’Europe, berceau de la révolution industrielle, fut à la pointe des grandes découvertes qui ont façonné le monde moderne. Aujourd’hui, néanmoins, nous avons raté le virage numérique, dépassés par les nouveaux géants que sont les États-Unis et la Chine, et nous ne rattraperons pas notre retard sans retrouver cet esprit européen qui fut jadis notre moteur. Or, nous connaissons tous ici la formidable capacité de la Commission européenne à innover dans un seul domaine: celui de générer toujours plus de normes, qui étouffent cet esprit créatif européen.

Alors oui, la prudence est de mise, mais pas à n’importe quel prix. Rien ne servira d’imposer des normes contraignantes à des entreprises que nous n’aurons jamais réussi à développer. Rien ne servira de parler de résilience si nous dépendons toujours de pays tiers dans les domaines des nouvelles technologies. Nous resterons donc vigilants à ce que la Commission ne se serve pas de la cybersécurité pour justifier son inaction, d’autant plus que, en risquant d’étouffer nos entrepreneurs, la Commission pourrait aussi écraser les innovations européennes en matière de cybersécurité.
2-0337-0000.englishText:
Mr President, dear colleagues, every contribution to technological innovation, every human progress has always been accompanied by its share of risks and new vulnerabilities. Artificial intelligence will be no exception.

Motivated by centuries of experience in technological risks, we would be well advised to ensure that AI does not become a new source of dependency for our nations. Europe, the cradle of the industrial revolution, was at the forefront of the great discoveries that shaped the modern world. Today, however, we have missed the digital turn, overtaken by the new giants that are the United States and China, and we will not catch up without rediscovering that European spirit which was once our engine. Yet we all know here the formidable capacity of the European Commission to innovate in a single field: that of generating ever more standards, which stifle this European creative spirit.

So yes, caution is called for, but not at any price. It will be of no use to impose binding standards on companies that we will never have managed to develop. It will be of no use to talk about resilience if we still depend on third countries in the fields of new technologies. We will therefore remain vigilant to ensure that the Commission does not use cybersecurity to justify its inaction, especially since, by risking stifling our entrepreneurs, the Commission could also crush European innovations in cybersecurity.

2-0338-0000.sourceText:
